Tea d Al Sir Andrew Clarke, For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroli,oratea *pinion. Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital: "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what! should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into a place, the lady of the house will say to me : 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a Cup of tea.' I say ' thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so no% ertul in its effects upon the nary nis system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. It you want to have, either for yourselves or for your Patients. tea which will not injure and which will refresk, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspoooful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour it off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for- gotten what this old fashioned tea is like. "

-•—• The colour of the tea after it is brewed will be found tobe much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to its apparent insipidness ; but if its use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to be much more suitable for the system. and if, in a week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have bean using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. - - - SIR ROBERT PEEL, on the occasion of a ministerial fish dinner, after he had ousted the Whigs, gave as a toast, "May we keep their plaices without their flounders." 1111: chief magistrate of an English borough recently received a petition addressed "To the Mare and Body Corpulent r It was written by a country schoolmaster. A BOARD of Guardians, having advertised for a schoolmaster, received an " application " from a candidate of "good charictor," who said he "could fill up his time at taloring," if required. A WAG who had taken refuge in a friend's house during v. recent storm, was asked if he would take a glass of porter. "No, I thank you," he replied, "I can get plenty of hail outside."

The Pope is following the Home Rule debate in the House of Commons with great interest, and, according to a semi-official Papal newspaper, has had several interviews with the new Irish Cardinal Logue on the subject. It is said that the Pope de- sires to thoroughly study all the aspects and phases of the problems in the solutions of which Irish Catholics are concerned. We probably shall have to wait until Cardinal Logue returni to his flock, before the drift of these conversations are known to the world.

" Mary 111. of England and Scotland "—as the Jacobites call their Queen over the water—does not seem to have regarded with any great sympathy the recent demonstrations of her English " fol- lowers." The Archduchess Marie-Therese of Modena is now fair, fat, and forty-four, and, though aware of her rights if the" Stuarts come back again," gets much more solid comfort out of the fact that her ' husband, Prince Louis, is the heir to the throne of Bavaria. She has ten children, the eldest. the Pretender Prince of Wales, being in his twenty- fourth year, a heavy fellow mentally, and as unlike "Bonnie Prince Charlie " as it is possible for man to be unlike another. The Archduchess is the near- est direct living descendent of James 11.

A SIGN-BOARD in the window of a fishmonger has the following curious invitation to the salmon tribe, who may have unfortunately got into pickle —" Good accommodation for pickled salmon. "HERE TO-DAY, AND GONE TO-MORROW."—To prove the veracity of this old saying, the reader need but invest a sovereign or two at any "respect- able" betting office.—Punch. A LONG NOSE.—An advertisement appeared in an American newspaper which read as follows : " Run away, a young man named Haggai, his nose turned up, five feet eight inches, and had on a pair of corduroy p:..nts, much worn." •

Dr. Benjamin Ward Richardson placed a high ideal of duty before the banqueting sanitary in- spector of London on Saturday night, when he adjured them to regard it as their mission to make the nation a garden of sweetness and light. He has himself—as Mr. John Hutton finely remarked— done much to realise his own ideals and towards answering his cwn prayers for the' Ilygeia," the model City of Health, which he outlined in a memorable address at Brighton some ten years ago. The later years of Dr. Richardson's professional career have been dedicated to the study of the special diseves incident to an expanding civilisa- tion ; and that he is now able to point with pride to the general adoption of sanitary schemes, once denominated visionary, must occasion him a lively satisfaction. mr--9

" Ho ! for California," seems to be the general cry all over the country—says the Philadelphia Sari. "Yes, and hoe for gold after you get there." Some go to California with a" ho" and return with "high-ho !" AN Australian farmer holds out temptations to Chelsea, Greenwich, and railway pensioners. He will give good wages and good fare to a class of servants who "cannot run away to the diggings"— that is, to wooden-legged emigrants. NOT ALONE WHEN ALONE.—" Billy Jones," said a bullying urchin to another lad, "next time I catch you alone, I'll flog you like anything."— "Well," replied Bill, "I ain't often much alone; I sommonly have my legs and my fista with me." A NEGRO'S DEFINITION OF A GENTLEMAN.— "Massa mak de black man workee—mak de horse werkee —make de ox workee—make everything workee, only de hog • de hog no workee ; he eat, he drink, he go to sleep when he please, he liff like a gentleman.'' THERE is a man in Vermont who is so attached to the principles of the Peace Society that he will not have a single flower in his garden, for "it's terrible," he says, "to walk out at this time of the year, and to see the flowers in all directions with shooting pistils." "I SEE (said a young lady the other day), that some stationers advertise blank declarations for sale; I wish I could get one." "Why ?" asked her mother.—" Because, ma, Mr. Green is too modest to ask me to marry him; and, perhaps, if I could fill up a blank declaration with the question he would sign it." SOME poetaster wrote the following : "Long is that morn that brings to eve ; tall is the corn that no cobs leave ; blue is the sky that never looks yeller; hard is the apple that never grows meller ; but longer, and bluer, and harder and tall, is my own lady love —my adorable Poll."—P.S. The author has since died in great agony. A NEW CANDIDATE.—It is said that Mr. Camp- bell of Monzie, in pursuing his canvas, called on an elector to ask his vote. To the surprise of the hon, candidate, the elector said emphatically, "No; I would sooner give it to the d—l." Mr. Camp- bell coolly replied, "Then after you hale voted for yom• favourite candidate, I trust you will give use your second vote !" Exit Monzie ! RELICS.—Horace Walpole relates that on his travels he met with an itinerant monk (evidently from the sister isle) who lived by showing some sacred relics he had. These were, a feather from St. Michael's wing, a crow from St. Peter's cock, a groan from Mary Magdalen, and, as the pious father expressed it, "a small bit of the blessed fig- tree which our Saviour cursed.' SILENCING A BlSHOP.—Jarvis, the painter, was painting Bishop —, and the venerable prelate began to remonstrate with him upon the dissipated course into which he had fallen. Jarvis, dropping his pencil from the forehead of his portrait to the lower part of his f:ace, said, with a slight motion to the reverend sitter, "Just shut your mouth, bishop!" By Fainting upon that feature he changed the subject. A KENTUCKY LAWYER'S APPEAL. "The thunder rolled, the moon robed, the stars winked, the sky was a complete wed—gentlemen of the jury—of darkling darkness on that night; and yet this 'ere man did, with malice aforethought, steal folth inter tile quiet shades of a lonely farmers' house, and theis maliciously pisened his brindle yallar dog. Convict him, and the prayers of a nation are yours!" Is reading over the prospectus of a new Insurance Society in the course of formation, the following rather singular and amusing clause was brought before our notice and runs as follows :—" Life Policies indisputable, and not liable to forfeiture, except in the event of the assured dying by their own hands, or by the hands of justice, or going out of the limits of Europe, or dying on the high seas, without the previous permission of the Court of Directors." SOME years ago, a servant girl who had robbed ner mistress, a milliner in London, was transported to Sydney for a term of years. Since the discovery of the Bathurst plains the female convict has written to her former mistress that the colony was a good place—that, as she now kept her carriage, she was happy to return the amount which she had stolen, with interest—that she earnestly recom- mended her to come out and set up shop, and that in that case she should he happy to extend her patronage to a lady for whom she had so great an esteem!

Madame ue Lesseps has done much by her spirited and compassionate defence of her aged husband—spirited as against his enemies, compas- •iionate as regards himself -r-to answer the criticisms of her life-long enemies in France. She is a Creole, and was a modest governess in Belgium when she attracted the attention of Le Grand Frangais. lier beauty and talent fascinated him, and, despite the violent protests of M. Charles de Lesseps, won the then rather elderly widower. Her rivals in Paris ; stigmatised her as an adventuress ; and, for some years at least, there seemed ground for the wittic- isms flung at the lady that she endeavoured to make ! up for the brevity of her decolletil costume by the length of her prayers. But with advancing years her traducers have become silent, and, while there is no doubt of her extravagance, none can doubt her simple devotion to M. Ferdinand de Lesseps.

- There are signs of renewed activity in the Duke of York's house in St. James's Palace. A work- shop has been fitted up on the ground floor, in which there is a good deal of work in process of completion. Of course the house was finished long op, but there are always odd jobs to be done, if only in the way of repairs, especially when a house remains empty for some time. We hear on good authority that the Duke of York confided to a friend that his visit to Osborne was one of no ordinary im- portance. The opinion favoured in society now is that the visit was connected with obtaining the Queen's formal sanction to the engagement, but that by her Majesty's special wish it was arranged that there should hero formal announcement of the engagement until after tile date which was once fixed for the wedding of the Duke of Clarence.

Mr. Caleb Wright, M.P., probably owes his life to John Burns. He was thrown down in the rush for seats on Monday,and was being trodden under foot, when the member for Battersea discovered his danger, and thrusting members right and let,made his way to Mr. Wright and picked 11:-n up. Mr. Wright, who represents the Leigh divisiou of Lan- cashire, is in his eighty-third year, and has sat for the same division since 1885. He is a self-made man,being the son of a clerk at Tyldesley,near Man- cbester,and one of thirteen children. At nine years of age Mr. Wright began work in a cotton factory, and continued to work in the same factory until thirty years of age. Five years later he went into business for himself at Tyldesley as a cotton spin- ner, was successful, an to-day has the hohour of representing the place in which he was born, began work, started business, and now resides.

-- An entertaining anecdote of the school days ot the Bishop of Carlisle! (the Rev. Dr. Bardsley, pre- viously Bishop of Sodor and Man) was related at the annual gathering of the Manchester Grammar School Old Boys" the other night. One day the French master when wishing to use the blackboard discovered that he had no chalk. Consequently someone had to go out to buy a piece. Young Bardsley was selected for this errand,and he sallied forth and called at one or two places but was un- successful in his quest. One shopkeeper at last persuaded him to take some pipeclay instead, and as he told the boy it would do as well, Master Bardsley repaired with it to the French master with all speed. The pipeclay, however, only marked the board with scratches, and, becoming very angry the master threw it away, at the same time casting a withering look at the boy and remarking " Thank you " Monsieur Pipeclay." After that the boys dubbed the future bishop " Pipeclay.' Mr. G. M. Whipple, the late superintendent of Kew Observatory, who was buried on Saturday in the Richmond Cemetery, was a man of the people. He was always a busy student, even as a boy in the Kingston Grammar School. As a meteorologist he had probably no compeer. His speciality was wind force and wind velocities. It is a study which de- mands the very highest powers of observation, united with the greatest patience. No doubt the severity of his labours was primarily responsible for his death at the early age of fifty. Beyond his unique meteorological attainments he was greatly valued in the wide scientific circle of frieniship he ' had formed, for the unpretentiousness of his man- ner, his quick sympathies, and his charmingly equable temperament. He is a great loss to the West , London district, for his popular scientific lectures were nearly always given on behalf of some deserv- ing institution,he himself never taking a penny.

A NEW ELECTIONEERING DODGE.—An enter- .prising grocer, of Cheapside, Lancaster, intends to stand up for the "rights of women" at the -ensuing borough election, in a somewhat novel way. The gentleman in question has commenced taking the opinion of each of his female customers upon the mcrits of the respective candidates, and he daily records the number of votes upon "a poll," exhibited in the window of his shop. Upon the day of election, he proposed to cast up the numbers given for each candidate, and to give his own vote for the two gentlemen most in favour with the ladies. —Lancaster Guardian. JCST LIKE PADDY.—A short time since a stal- wart Patlander paid :a visit to a gentleman's man- sion, the object of his call being, of course, for the purpose of—begging. Contrary to his usual good breeding, Pat went "right forward" into the sanctum of his butlership, who, in a burst of indignation, asked him what brought him there. "Och," i,ald Paddy, "an' it's that ye're axin', is it? Shure, thin, an' it was to spake with ye're honours glory."—" Well, then, sir," retorted the butler, "110 you not know that, according to the rules of this house, it is customary before coming in to knock at the door?"—" Arrah, by me sow!," bawled Paddy, "an' how should I known the rule -of the house until I came in to ax?" 'the man of the cellar was nonp:ussed, and rewarded Pat with a " drop of something" for his wit. DllELLlNG.—Trawiling in a stage-coach, Pro. fessor Viace got into an argument with a fellow. traveller about duelling, the necessity of which the professor strenuously denied. The other as stoutly supported it, cud insisted that there were many cases which could only be decided by a duel. "I deny that,' said the professor.—" Pooh," replied the other, " quite clear. Why, what else can you do? Here are you and I talking together; and suppose we get into a warm argument, anal say to you, You lie'? what can you do then? You must light me. Ttere's no other remedy."—" I deny it," with a provoking coolness replied the professor.— " Well, but what can you do?"—" Why," he again replied, "if you say to me, You lie,' I ligould say Prove it. If you prove it, Ido lie ; if you don't prove it, it's you that lie. And there's an end of the matter," A GENTLE HINT.—He had been courting her a long time, so long that she began to get tired ; so one night she said to him : " John, who is the anther of the phrase, Man proposes ?' " "I'm sure I doi.'t know," answered John. "Why do you ask?" "Oh I I merely wanted to know who h,e was." "For what reason?" " Because I guess he dia'nt know what he was talking about." Mr." Pony " Moore, whose name is now being I brcught rather prominently before the public in consequence of the changes taking place in his famous" nigger show," has had a long and varied career. His father was a drummer in the American army. There were thirteen in the family, and Mr. Moore was the youngest of the lot. He began to earn his living as a circus performer, his work being to drive forty ponies. It was through this that he earned the sobriquet which has stuck to him since he was twelve years of age. " Pony " did not take , to nigger minstrelsy till the year 1846, and then he used to go about solus and tune up his banjo on steam and ferry boats. He came to England in 1859, and has played here ever since, starting with quite a small troupe. For ten years Mr. Moore never missed a night, and when he began to take holidaysthey never extended over three or four weeks Surely a man who has "worked at play" like this fully merits the success that has crowned his efforts.

By the death of the Rev. Francis Orpen Morris, rector of Menburnholme, the county of broad acres loses its most versatile and distinguished natura- list. At the ripe age of eighty-three this typical Yorkshireman has passed away from the active life of the Riding which he loved so well. Though not remarkable when at Worcester College, Oxford, for more than a youthful love of bird's eggs and coun- try life, Mr. Morris graduated in honours sixty years ago, and took orders shortly after. Ever since he has been an industrious worker and proli- fic writer. Mr. Morris simply revelled in ornitho- logy. The long list of works which he has issued during the last fifty years records the result of keen observation and patient research. Entirely free from worldly ambition, this worthy parson was content to pass his time in the quiet seclusion of his country rectory, amid books and birds, daily communings with nature, and pleasant chats with his attached parishioners,whose joys and woes he made his own. Open-handed and kind-hearted, Mr. Morris was a i humane magistrate, a true friend to the sick and suffering, and as fond of a good story as he disliked • touting for the" loaves and fishes "of the Estab- lished Church.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1893.
LADIES' LETTER
MY DEAR NELLIE,

In Paris I am told fur, guipure, and artificial flowers are now employed very much together in millinery; and dainty theatre bonnets of wired guipure have no other trimming than a brim of fur, two little upstanding ears of the same, and a bunch of spring flowers nestling cosily at their base. Wings, too, are greatly in favour, to which are added the " pattes," or claws of birds, oxydised, silvered, or gilt. A hat of brown felt, trimmed in the front with the bouquet of affrighted songsters' feathers in tones of green and fawn, was garnished also with the claws thrust forth and bronzed in green and gold. The effect, although novel, sug- gested home-made pigeon pie. Violets, primroses, t.nd twigs of ntahonia bloom and leaves, together with gigantic dragon flies, are the favourite bonnet and hat trimmings of the present moment, while tiny " toquets " of shaded velvet are considered very smart for evening wear, carelessly knotted in "msrmotte " fashion, with two upstanding ears of velvet.

The revival necklets has brought to light many pretty things in lapidaries' and jewellers, art. The smartest idea in this form is a deep collar of pearls intersected at intervals by bars of diamonds. As many as seven rows of large Oriental pearls are thus worn, and the collar is fastened with a solid square clasp, encrusted with diamonds. There is no arbitrary law as to neck. lets, a—nd for this /ve have reason to be deeply thankful, since Nature has provided necks of such widely differing character. The liossessor of one formed in long, graceful, swan-like proportions may with impunity venture on a collar cl Tp and massive, and be sure that it suits her to perfection. If, however, a lady of more plump dimensions and a short, white throat were to buckle round it so etiff a piece of jewellery she would assuredly appear to be strangled by her own mannificence. A necklet in graceful festoons of pearls caught up by rosettes of diamonds, and having perhaps alternate pendants of black and white pear-shaped pearls, would suit such a wearer as perfectly as the stiffer collars would suit her differently constructed sister.

What must be just as interesting to the bride as her wedding dress is the going away costume. A recent bride wore a mantle in departing for her honeymoon which, especially in this weather, made one positively envious. It was of smoke grey mirror velvet lined with pale green. The feature of the mantle, however, was the unique trimming of finest darkest Imperial Russian sable which formed the collar and cuffs, and bordered the floats and the e ige, the depth of the latter being just the length of the sable skin. ‘Ve may look for a season of bright rich colour, combined with darker shades. As the innovation of different hued velvet puffs, fur sleeves, and large collars to evening gowns made a revolution in ball-rooms and turned them into scenes of kaleidoscopic variety of colour, SD we may expect brilliancy in tone in day dress to a much greater extent than we had it throughout list year. A dress of pale grey cloth has sleeves and a square bib, back and front, of the brightest and richest shade of violet velvet. Another gown in black fancy material, flecked over with tiny dots in scarlet, has sleeves of this brilliant-hued velvet, and a folded belt to match, while the black felt eavalier hat has a scarlet ostrich plume laid along the drooping brim. As the spring advances the colours chosen will be more delicate, and the materials naturally lighter; but there is every reason to believe that which clever colourists have inaugurated will prove to be both long and success- ful. Nevertheless, one need not go to bright colours always for pretty costumes. A toilette de visite of brown cloth, with sleeves of apricot, velvet, arranged in triple cape style with bodice and skirt trimmed with narrow bands of fur, was very attractive.

A petson with a long face should never dress the hair high upon the held. The eff..ct is to increase the apparent length of the features—the very thing which is to be avoided. The proper disposition, therefore, is to comb the hair smoothly at the top of the head, letting it roll somewhat at the sides, so as to add to the apparent breadth of the features. A lady dressed with a short, rather broad face, will naturally gather her tresses at the top of her head; if her brow be low, the hair will combed up from it, leaving it full, natural height; while if it be higher than is desired, the hair is deftly made to cover a portion of the expanse. if the brow is too wide, a little curl or some other appropriate dressing at the sides serves as a correc- tive; while a little range of curls beneath the back hair, attractive in themselves, also very often serves to decrease the apparent length of the wearer's neck.
Yours ever, JErusTrE
The Empress of Russia makes all the clothing for her younger children, and also trims their new hats to suit hr own taste.

At the time of the Flood the women of Babylon were arrayed in headgear and dresses almost the same as the styles now fashionable. This is proved by en- graved stones and monuments stored in the British Museum.

As regards the gossip about the Princess of Wales and the crinolines, they are very much disliked by the Princess and the ladies of her household, and are not at all likely to come into fashion with them again.

Stewed Liver and Bacon.

Sheep's liver, llb: (sliced) ; fat bacon, en. or lb.; onion, one (sliced) ; flour, one tablespoonful; water, one pint. Seasoning of pepper and salt. Slice the bacon, put it in a saucepan over the fire, add the onion, when lightly browned (but on no account burned), pour in the water, and when it boils, put in the liver. Let it simmer very gently for nearly an hour. Take out the liver and bacon, put it on • a hot dish and keep it hot while the gravy is thickened with flour, and seasoned, then pour it round the fiver and bacon, and serve.

div.head: Treacle Roll.
div.p: Treacle Roll.

Suet pastry, treacle, bread crumbs. Roll out the paste about three-quarters or half-an inch thick; spread the middle thickly with treacle, and on this scatter bread crumbs. Roll it up in the shape of a bolster; fasten it firmly in a scalded and floured cloth. Boil two hours.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHURCH.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHURCH.

The " Manchester Guardian" of Saturday gives an excellent illustration of Warrington Parish Church, and also contains the following account by Mr. Alfred Rimmer, which reads as follows "The present church of Warrington has been al- most entirely rebuilt. The church taken down was a large cruciform structure. The tower, rising from the intersection of the transepts, was built in William lll.'s reign. The nave with its aisles and south transept was completed in 1770, and its large I windows were built in the Italian style of.architec- ture that had come so.completely into vogue; the Ichancel dated back to about 1357. Part of this chancel• still remains. On the north side of the chancel is a heavy buttress containing a staircase that went up about half the height of the chancel wall from the crypt. This is a unique specimen, and its object is not known. The tower, which was large, was adorned with battlements and contained six bells. Many Nerman relics were found, which are now in the Museum. A cl urch was in existence here at the Con- quest, and is mentioned in Domesday Book ; it was de- dicated to St. Elphin. In ancient documents it is called the" High Kirk" and the saint is not named. The spire of the present church is out of proportion. It is a great contrast to the finely proportioned tower of Walton, which is near. The latter was the work of Paley: The work of reconstruction was begun in 1859 and finished in 1887. The spire is 281 feet high. The exterior of the new church is not all that could be desired, but the interior is a fine one. The organ is at the west end, an unusual position, though there can be no doubt that in the majority of cases ,the west end is the best place for the instrument.

Warrington Church is a rectory, and in the year 1291 it was put down at the value of £l3 6s. Bd. per annum. There was a singular presentation of Warrington Church with its income to the priory and canons of Thingarton, Nottingham. This was granted by Sir Mathew de Villers and his brothers, and the donation was confirmed by Sir William Boteler, and would date back to the beginning of Edwatd L's reign. There are two old chantries in the church—the Bewsey Chapel and the Rixton, now called the Patten Chapel, where Lord Winmarleigh, the head of the Fattens, was re- cently interred. These are on the north side of the tower, and almost opposite to each other. On the south side of thQ chancel there is a marble monument to the celebrated Dr. Percival, with an inscription written by De. Parr. In the Bewsey chantry there is a fine tomb of Sir John Botelor and his wife. In the Patten Chapel there are many beautifully sculptured tablets!, memorials of members of the Patten family. At the time of the Re- formation there were two chantries here, but they were of course suppressed. One was founded by Sir William Butler, but endowed by Sir Thomas Butler; indeed it is called the latter's own foundation by the Royal Commis- sioners. He appointed an honeste priest learned in Grammar, to be master, who should say Mass, pray,and do divine service at the Parish Church of Warrington, for the soul of him, the said Sir Thomas,Da me Margaret, his wife, his ancestors, and heirs.' Robert Hall was the chantry priest,and he had a pension of £4 is. 4d. a year. There was another chantry at the altar of St. Anne, founded by Rector Delves, whcse sister was the Dame Margaret mentioned above. The church has a spacious yard, filled with gravestones and still containing trees. Warrington was at one time the most important publish- ing town in Lancashire. The first, Lancashire newspaper was published here,and Howard's celebrated work show- ing the shocking condition of the prisons in his time was produced at Warrington. Here also the earlier writings of William Roscoe were published, as well as the poems of Mrs. Barbauld. The trades of Warrington derive great advantage from its position in the centre of a manufac- turing district ; and though until recently only vessels of 70 or 80 tons burthen could reach the town, the Ship Canal will make its docks available for vessels of a con- siderably larger draught.

PROFESSOR BLACKIE'S OPINION OF SCOTSMEN AND ENGLISHMEN. Professor Blackie, speaking in Dundee, said he had never seen a more beautiful city than Edin- burgh. Princes-street, for instance, was out of sight the finest Street in the world. All the same, there was less Scottish feeling in Edinburgh than in any other town in Scotland, and it all arose from big-wiggery. (Laughter.) The lawyers • did not require any sentiment ; they were merely intellec- tual fencing nal:whines. (Laughter.) They, all looked up to London as the plebe to go to, to go and get bigger and bigger and come back with a bigger wig than ever. (Laughter and applause.) People talked a lot about reading, and they read silly books, and read all the gossip in the newspapers. One good Scottish song was worth all the gossip of the world. (Applause.) A lot of newspapers were Idled with such stories of murders and blasphemieS as would almost make one think the world was the introduction to hell. When he went into a railway aarriace he did not begin to read he just hummed to himself a guid auld Scotch sang. (Applause.) Next to the-blessed Gospel a goad Scotch song in the heart and soul of a Scotchman was better than much of what was called learning. Reading was only for record. He knew something about books ; he had 7,000 volumes in his library—and he said reading was a stupid thing. When people were stupid they could not do anything better than read. (Laughter.) When the young fashionable West End lady returned from the ball she could not do anything but read. (Laughter.) A man was fully alive when he sang, and then he became like a bird. Pros 2 was extremely useful, but extremely dull ; poetrY was a bickering mountain-stream flashing in the sunshine. Song ought to be the main element of all education ; a man was imperfect until he felt himself in his soul becoming a bird. They would find that in ancient times song was the main eitpression of the noblest feelings. There were the Psalms of David ; and then, too, they danced. That, however, was not a Scot- tish custom as far as religion was concerned. A map who was thoroughly happy sang and danced, and the man who could neither sing nor dance as a poor, pitiful kind of a creature. (Laughter.) He was not a right kind of a-man unless he understood that piety and gaiety should go together—devotion and song, In Scot- land religion was a rather sour thing. Some Scotchmen tried to make their spiritual heaven as gloOmy and as cloudy as their Scottish sky. The D.D.'s had a lot to do with that.—(Hear, hear.) They pretended te know the Bible, and they did not know it at all.—("Hear,hear,"and laughter.) In the Bible religion was always ccupled with gaiety, and, as he said before, even with dancing. He should like to see a couple of old D.D.'s dancing, and yet these D.D.'s swore by the Psalms of Dauvit. The Bible told them to praise the Lord with music. How- ever, he would have to go on with his lecture. He could go on that way tor ever on that subject. He just felt like a mountain burn coming down from Ben Cruachan. —(Applause) Did it never occur to them that the char- acteristics of Scottish people began with the letter S There were songs, stories, shillings—(laughter),—ser- mons, and steam, and then shrewdness, sagacity, and so on. There was one thing, he wished to warn them against, and that was the worshipping of material mag- nitude. John Bull was a respectable sort of a creature with a big, paunch—(langhter),—and he had as many people in London as there were in Scotland. The Scotch were, he considered, superior to the English, and he would ask his hearers to beware of those things which would make them forget themselves and become wor- shippers of a people morally not so noble as themselves. —(Applause.)—He asked them to beware of looking to London. The Anglified puppies and prigs of girls were always looking to London and away from Scotland.— (Laughter and applause.)—He had a notion that the so- called aristocracy were not Scotch. A great many of them were Episcopalians, and no Episcopalian was a true Scotchman. The Professor then told in his own characteristic fashion the story of Jenny Geddes, and then proceeded with his lecture. He concluded by cit- ing examples of love' patriotic war, and convivial songs. They must not think that convivial songs meant drink- ing songs. They did not. The moment they got drunk they could not sing.—(Applause.) Therefore it was that these songs helped to keep them sober. No drunken man could sing. (Applause.) He thought he had better stop, las he had an idea that he had done very well for an old gentleman of 83 years and five months.

div.head: DARK WOOD.
div.p: DARK WOOD.
A TALE OF LONEMOOR.
TIY MRS. HARRIETT LEWIS, Author of •• The Smidered Hearts," "The tailiff's Scheme," "The Double Life," &c.
CHAPTER XI. INTERFERENCE.

Claxton Orkney was rather pleased than other- wise at the unexpected display of Owens fearless- ness and spirit. Knowing her secret history he had expected, despite her avoidance of him, to make an easy conquest of her. Her opposition only fired his zeal and quickened his determination to possess her. "What a little spitfire she is," he etelaimed ad- miringly. "But I never liked a tame eat. You must have seen, Gwendoline, that I admire you and love you. I have seen many women in my time, but not one that can compare with you." "And this is what you wish to tell me ?" demanded Gwen haughtily. . "Yes, this and more. Your life can't he happy at Lonemoor. Mrs. Quillet is more like a death's head in these days than a woman. You live alone in that great house, scowled and frowned upon, and I won er that you endure it. I love you Gwen. Let me take you away from Lonemoor. 111 make you happy. I'll surround you with luxuries. You shall live in London, or wh:re you like. I'm think- ing of going back to town. In fact, it is my love for you that has kept me here. My father will give me a sum of money to start me in he, and you shall live in luxury. Will you go with me, Gwendeline ?" "Miss Winter, if you please "said the girl coldly. "And to your question, no, 311 x. Orkney.' "Why not? I love you--" "But I don't love you," said Gwen. " Love may come in time," urged her suitor. "If not, I'll be content with your liking. Think of London with its theatres, op:-ras and shops. Think of a house of your own, Gwendoline, and no one to look sourly at you. I've set my heart on you. Won't you give yourself to me ?" "It is impossible. I have given you one good and sufficient reason, which ought to havd con- tented you. I don't love you, and should never learn to love you, Mr. Orkney, not if I should try a thousand years. But I have another reason;' and Gwen's proud face flushed. "I would never marry into your family. never. I would not be- come daughter-in-law to your mother, or sister-in- law to your sisters for all the money in England." "Daughter-in-law! Sister-in-lawl" echoed young Orkney, blankly. Something in his tone as well as in the words startled Gwen, bringing the hot blood to her cheeks and a strange light to her purple dark eyes. "Were you not soliciting me to become a relative to your relatives ?" she demanded. "Did you not ask me to marry you ?" The young man was silent for a moment. "Did I ?" he then asked insolently. If a look could have killed then Gwen would have slain him upon the spot. White as death she shrank away from him, her thin nostrils dilating, her mouth expressing a scorn that was withering. Hou4nl j', she said, and the word cut the villain lash. "I shall write to Squire Markham by the first post. I can safely leave you to hie vengeance.' Orkney laughed sneeringly. "You think so?" he said. 'Come. come, Gwen- dolize. It is time you laid aside these airs and graces. You speak of appealing to Squire Markham. Why, he doesn't even know of your existence. If he knew how you are queening it at Lonemoor he'd turn you and the Quillets out on the instant—if he didn't send you to gaol. You appeal to Squire Markham? 'You? That is rich Why, by gad, do you know who you are ?" "I know who you are,' answered Gwen. low, pitiful hound. Let me pass." "Not yet?" cried Orkney in a rage. "I mean to humble your proud spirit. I mean to tell you who you are. By heaven, I'll make you glad to accept my offer. Why do people look at you as they do ! Why do they avoid your acquaintance? Why, since your return to Lonemoor, do the neighbours shun the Quillets ? Can't you guess? Its on your account. You are the leper from whom all shrink.' _ _
"A

" Von ! 11l tell you the whole story,' said Orkney savagely. "lye known it always. And when you know you'd jump at my offer, and beg me to take you away from this place, where every one knows your history. But before I tell you, I must have a kiss from those proud lips. They I won't be so proud after my story is told. A kiss, my princess.' He bounded towards her, caught her, nround the waist and b_nt his face to hers. The girl struggled like a mad creature, and dashed her little fist full into his mouth. Smarting with pain, furious with rs.ge, exerting all his brut-3 strenth, the villain seemed fairly to crush her in his creep. But before he could snatch the kiss he threatened, or defile her pure lips with his touch, there was a sudden rush as of a whirlwind, a pair of strong hands seized upon him, and he was burled to the ground. In their excitement and self-absorption neither , 3wen nor her enemy had noticed the approach of a 1 roung sportsman, who, equipped with bag and gun, 1 Lppeared tobe upon a solitary shooting expedition. I lie had, in fact, separated from his party an hour alck, and was in search of game, when upon strik- ng the high road he came upon the little scene we save described. A single glance showed him that Gwen and her :omparnon were not upon friendly terms. The Lttitude of the former Was defiant, that of the tatter aggressive and violent. The stranger drew I Seater. Then came young Orkney's sudden assault I apon the girl, and her resistance—and then the ' stranger took part in the affair with the effect narrated. For it was the sound of his approach that resembled the rush of a whirlwind; it was his hand that seized the villain and hurled him to the ground. Orkney staggered to his feet, maddened and com- bative, and with a muttered curse rushed upon his assailant. The latter knocked him down three times in suc- cession in the coolest possible manner, as Orkney again and again returned to the charge. The villain, bruised and bleeding, finally regained an upright position, and having learned wisdom from defeat, stood apart, sullen, angry, and malig- nant, staring at the stranger with a glance of ab- solute hatred. "Can I do anything more for you I' inquired the latter pleasantly, Orkney measured the frame of his antagonist with his eyes. The latter was tall, slender, and active, about twenty-four years of age, with a dauntless, resolute face, and a figure compactly knit and combining unusual measure of strength and grace. Just now his eyes were flashing, his mouth wore a smile of contempt, and his appearance impressed Orkney al formidable. The latter evinced a desire to retire from the contest. ".Mount," said the stranger authoritatively, yet With an amused' smile,." and go." His advice really seemed excellent under the cir- cumstances. Nothing but further bruises was to be gained by a prolonged stay. Orkney concluded to depart, his resolution receiving force from the fact that the waggonette had halted in the distance, and four feminine heads were craned backwards in an endeavour o see "why that horrid beggar was detaining our Claxton." It seemed very probable that the three common- place Orkney girls and their commonplace mamma would turn about and swoop down upon the girl whom they believed to be alluring their brother and son to his destruction. Certainly wisdom diet tated Otknev's immediate retreat, and he moved towards his horse. "We shall meet again," he said, in a half-choked voice. "Your name—your name." The amused smile on the stranger's countenance assumed a mocking character. "Your friends have become alarmed for your safety," he said, "and are coming after you."

True enough the waggonette was returning. Orkney clambered into his saddle. Some insult- ing words in regard to Gwen's origin came to his lips, but he repressed them. He feared the strong arm of her defender. He feared his relatives' return, and he had by no means relinquished his designs in regard to Gwen. So, choking with rage, covered with blood and dust, he beat an inglorious retreat, leaving his assailant master of the situation. Gwen leaned against her horse, and with her new fri,nd watched Orkney's swift gallop, his meeting with the waggonette, his parley with his friends, and finally their retreat alto6ether in a homeward direction. Then the stranger turned to the young lady, say- ing, with a very different sort of smile from the last seen on his face : "The young man is disposed of, and no doubt you will take care that he d, es not molest you again. You are really venturesome to ride without an attendau

G wee wki trembling—more waft resentment it must be coofOssed, than fear. Her face was still pale, her oyes glowing like purple stars. The insults of Orkney had stirred her too deeply to permit an immediate: assumption of that repose of manner which is tmpposed to mark a lady of the caste of Vera de Vert: under any and all circumstances bat that Gwen was a lady, her every look and action,dier very attitude showed. She had not been named " Princess " without.good cause, and the youn2 man thought, as he regarded her, that she was the most beautiful and thoroughly well-bred girl he had ev r seen. "You hid better sit down on this boulder," he remarked. "All this has agitated you. I wonder you :didn't faint. :That is the usual resort of the young lady of the period , is it not ?" His light words 'tad the effeot he designed. They assisted to restore the giqs composure. . As she grew calmer, Gwen: disrovered, what she had not bad time to notice before, that her rescuer was very handsome, with a fair and noble face, a massive forehead, a pair of keen blue eyes, and a head covered over with close-curling rings of lair hair.

"Permit inn to Introduce myself," paid the young gentleman gravely. "Jam Ronald Chilton, a guest at the shooting lodge on the Lonemoor estate." "And I am Miss Winter of Lonemoor,' said Gwen. "I am very much obliged to you, Mr. Chilton, for your timely appearance and your brave defence of ma

"Permit me to see you home, Miss Winter," said Mr. Chilton, as Gwen arose. "It is not safe for you to go alone." The girl accepted his companionship, and he led the horse, while she walked slowly at his side in the direction of Lonemoor. Gwenrecoveredherstrength and her spirits in the clear, bracing air under the influence of his presence, and forgot for the time the dark hints her enemy had uttered concerning her secret history. It was a memorable walk, and long before they reached Lonemoor each had made upon the heart of the other an impression never to be effaced. Both were young, well educatel, refined, and in- telligent. Their tastes proved similar. Gwen was fresh frern school a very nun in her knowledge of the would. Mr. Chilton was university bred, knew the world, but was pure in heart and in life, chival- rous in the extreme, with a reverence for woman- ho' d rarely .to be found in these degenerate days. Gwen w..lked for a mile or two and then mounted her•pony. Mr. Chilton continued at her side, and the potty shambled along, cropping now and then at a weed or a thistle, and his young mistress, strange to say, scare&y noticed-Isis behaviour. The young pair talked of the moors, of flowers, then of books, and then of life and hopes and spec- ulations, and when the chimneys of Lonemoor ap- peared among t .e trees a pang of regret traversed each heart. How brief the distance had seemed. They halted at the go, eof Lonemoor. Gwen did not ask Mr. Chilton to enter' and after a few parting words he raised his hat and strode away with a free and graceful step. The girl rode into the Lonemoor grounds, and dis- mounted at a horsehloek near a side porch. A stablebov was vi,iolo in the direction of the stable- yard. Gwen beckoned to him, but he appeared not to notice her signal. She repeated it sharply, and he came forward ttl.iwly, with a slouching gait, as if quite indifferent to her req •irements. There was insnlence in his lazy movements and the saucy smile on his.face— an insolence, that Tought bat:li to Gweu the previous insults of young Orkney. With a sudden heightening of colour, she threw the reins upon her pony's neck, and he went at a keen run to the stables. Gwen entered at the door and ascended to her own rooms. ,

Her maid was not there and the girl did not • summon her. Her windows were open, her plants in full blossom and fragrance, and a cool dimness reigned. But it seemed to Gwen that the bloom had departed from her possessions. Those questions of Orkney rung in her ears. Wiso was she? What right had she here? Had she any right to those comfortable, nay, luxurious rooms? . .

She passed Into the dressing-room and changed her habit. Her maid had laid out for her use a pretty dress of pale blue woollen fabric, and Gwen put it on almost vrithout thinking. Her toilet was quickly xriccle, and the girl then went downstairs to the h usekeeper's room.
CHAPTER XII. THE REVELATION.

Mrs. Quillet was in her favourite flaunt, engaged In darning house linen. She had put on a pair of black-rimmed spectacles to assist her vision, and looked up over them at the girl with a cold and severe gaze. She saw at once that something had aappenee to her charge. Gwen's face was white and resolute, with a dash of sternness in the proud pained eyes, and a troubled wistfulness about the perfect mouth. "What's the matter?" demanded the housekeeper, fretfully. Has anything gone wrong ? Don't com- plain to me of the servants, Miss Gwendoline. I zan do nothing with them except discharge them, and they have been in the house so long I don't Like to do that."

"You have noticed the behaviour of the servants, then, Mrs. Quillet ?" "1? I have noticed nothing. Which one is in fault? Of course," added Mrs. Quillet, in a milder tone, "If the servants are tailing in respect they must go!' "I have no complaints to make, Mrs. Quillet," said Gwen quietly. "Had it really occurred to me that they were insolent I should have discharged them." Mrs. Quillet stared. "I supposed that I had the right to do so--that I was in truth mistress of Lonemoor " continued Gwen, in the same quiet tone. " Have I the rhht ? Am I mistress here ?" The houseke per was silent a moment, still regard- !ng the girl with that unchanging stare. "Who has been disputing your right?" she asked, after a little. "Whoe'has been talking to u?' "I met the younger Mr. Orkney upon the moor," said Gwen. "He insulted me grossly'!"

"Insulted you t' When I resented the insult he asked me who I was,' continued Gwen unheeding the interruption. "He said I had no right here. I never thought of the matier before. I spent my childhood in this house as if I had a right here. I had a governess here; I had the old family schoolroom which had been occupied by generations of Markhams ; I had a pleasant chamber that some of the family had owned before me ; I played in the gardens • I rode the horses; I plucked the flowers. No one forbade me these things. Of course, then, I supposed that I had a right her, What else could I think 1" The housekeeper did not answer. "I was sent lo a Paris remsionnat among the daughters of titled people. There were girls there who were my dear friends, and who were born to titles. I was considered their equal. I dressed as well as they. Madame de Loraine made no differ- ence between them and me. She said once that we were all well born, the daughters of gentlemen. I passed through the school course. I acquitted myself with honour. You came to bring me home. , I found here handsome rooms prepared for me. Of course I believed myself mistress of the house. What else could I think ?" She looked at the housekeeper steadily, with hex great purple blac:: eyes that were still full of pain, and the woman repeated her final question atter her tmoonscio u sly. 'Rave I been under a mistake all these years ?" the girl questioned. "rs there some mystery about I have accepted my life and all that it brotight me without question I I have wakened. The hour is come, Mrs. Quillet, when I demand of you a full explanation about myself. I demand this explam I ation as my right. Am I a relative of Squire Mark. I ham 2" _ _ _

The housekeeper, remembr ring that promise slit had given long years ago to the squire to keep fol ever the secret of Miss Markham's disgrace, remem bering that the sq ire would never achnowledg( any relationship to this nameless girl, she shook hei head dumbly. "What! Jam no relation to Squire Markham I am then his ward 1" _

Again the housekeeper shook her head. "Not his ward :" The girl grew paler. "II knew my parents, I suppose, and educated me be cause of friendship for them I" . Mrs. Quillet was still silent. "You do not answer," cried Gwen. "Did not &vire Markham know my father ." "No," answered the housekeeper, breaking bell silence in a strained voice. "Squire Markham neve' saw your lather, never knew his name, nor ever his nationality." Gwen looked shocked. She was very still fot some moments, but into those moments were cons pressed a thousand agonies. What could it all mean ' What hidden secrets was she about to uncovet Her heart seemed actually to stop its beatings ir the suspense and dread of her expectations. "How then has it happened that Squire Mark. ham has educated me in the manner h has done? she questioned in a hollow voice. "If he did not know my parents, how came he to care for me P' "He has not eared for you, Miss Gwendolina Jitieea 119 t e'en know. you are living,."
Gwen looked stunned. "How does it happen, then, that I am here i" sh( asked, after a little.

"The time has come for you to Lnnw the truth. Miss Gwendoline," said the house eeper. "I havt been an old fool to believe for an instant that it could he kept long from you. What I have done has been for the best. I meant to make your lif€ happy. Heaven knows I have acted as I thought wisely." She put her handkerchief to her eyes. "Yes," said Gwen, a little sharply, in her anxiety and dread; "but who am I, Mrs. Quillet,—whc am I?"

"Seventeen years ago, in November," said Mrs. Quillet, "on an awful night, in a storm that was terrible with sleet and wind, a woman—a girl I should say—came to this house for shelter. Upon that very night she gave birth to a child. A month afterwards, in a storm more terrible, when the moors were covered with snow, and the air was thick with the tia es, she fle from us, leaving the child behind her. The child was you, Gwendoline." "And the woman—my mother ?" "We sent men out to search for her, and they searched the night through the next day, and the next; but she was not to be found. In the April following, when the snow melted off the ground, they renewed the search and found her in a hollow where she had lain all the winter. She must have died in the storm on the very night of 1.1... r flight. We buried her at Penistone." "And my mother What was her name 7" "She never told her name, nor anything concern- ing herself. She was not in her right mind," said the house< eeper' hesitatingly, her tears dropping as she remembered the bright young mistress whom she had lost. "Poor child I She had never noticed anyone, not even her baby." Gwen walked to the window and loo',ed out. Not even the old housekeeper might loos upon her anguished features. "A stiange story," said the• girl, after another silence. "Tell me the rest, Mrs. Quillet, how Squire Markham befriended me, and--"

"He never saw your face. He left England about the time this happened. He never gave one penny towards your education." "Who did ?" cried Gwen quic ly. "John and I. We engaged and plicl your gov- erness out of our own savings; we sent you to Paris to school; we have doue everything ourselves. Now you understand, Miss Gwendolin the whole mystery. We brought you bac to Lonem,,or as our charge. You have really no right here, except such as we have given you." The girl's chee, s flushed hotly. . Then I have played the mistress here while I am in reality your dependent,' she exclaimed. "This is why the servants were slow to ohey ine. This is why the farmers sons 100 so strangely ,at me. Mrs. Quillet," and her voice grew ,harper with a sudden pain, "where is toy 'nether's wed- ding ring? Did you not keep it for me t'' The housecepers head was hidden, as she answered mournfully— " She wore no wedding ring l" No try tame from Gwen s lips. She bore he pain lilie a Spartan, for she ;was made of heroic stuff; but heaven and her own soul alone new the t een- ness of her ageay. . s

"I shali always believe that she was good and pure," said Mrs. Quillet, spea ing more to herpelf than to G wen. " She had suffered • she was thin, and haggard, and crazy, but I'lt not be:ie e that she was bad. An angel could not make me I;elie e it. _ .
The girl turned and ran swiftly towards the grin housekeeper, knelt beside her, caught up her bony hand, and kissed it with passionate for. our.
" I never knew before how good you were I" she exclaimed. 'I thank you in her name for your good words of her."
Mrs. Quinet drew away her hanl aryl wi6ecl it with her handkerchief. The tears and kisses upon it annoyed rather than pleased her. Of all things, she disliked emotion and hated a scene.

"Why have you done all this for me? ' criedGvven. " Why- did you educate me? Why did you Rot bring me up as a servant or a daughter 1" "It was our fancy, John's and mine," said the lousekeeper confusedly. "Your mother was a lady —there's no denying that—and we decided to bring op her child as a lady." You were very good," said Gwen, humbly. "I inn never repay you. But I ought not to live here is mistress of this house, when in reality I have no right here. I cannot wear these fine garments while you wear cheap ones. I cannot be served in the dining-room while you eat here. I cannot occupy these handsome chambers while your rooms are humble. What shall I do to show you my:. gratitude and love? Mrs. Quillet, my benefao tress—" "'Get up off your knees, Miss Gwendoline," said the old woman nervously. "Some one may come. What I did was not for you. I did it for your,v mother's sake. I—l took a fancy to her, you see., Do got up, Miss Gwen." Gwen rose slowly. "It is all a strange mystery to me,'!. the said girl, with a long breath. "A frightful mystery. oman comes out of the storm leaving a child be- hind her, and no one knows who that woman is nor, whence she came. And she died with her story, ; untold. Did no one ever come in search of her t - Did no one ever advertise for her ?" "No one." "My name—how did I come by that r • , "We called you Gwendoline because the name had been in the Markham family and was pretty. , The other name was invented. It was a wintrY, nig•.t when you came. We couldn't give you oaril name, nor yet any real name. So we called you Winter.' . • "And I have no name of my very own. You' gave me my name as you gave me my food and clothes ?"

" The same." "You never loved me," said pocr Gwen, in s desolate voice. "You did all this for my mother's sake, and she was crazy, and you did not know her real name or identity. You have heart of gold, , Mrs. Quillet, under all your seeming hardness. For your goodness to her and to me I will be your servant—your slave,'' She made a movement to stoop, as if -again t& kiss the housekeeper bony hand; but at that „ juncture a thundering knock was heard upon the door, and the bailid strode into the room. His face was red and inflamed with anger. JO • looked severe and uncompromising, and his glances sought out Gwen at once, she being the object of his visit. "Mrs. Quillet," he said, in a dictatorial lA:4°a; 411 am come here to complain of your—your ward. Gwen returned to the window. " Won't you sit down, Mr. Orkney I" asked the housekeeper. " No. lam here on bisineis, not to visit," Ws° the answer. "My family went to Penistone to-daY on a shopping excursion. The ladies went in a waggonette, and my son accompanied them en horseback. On their return they encountered Yelir Gwendoline, who was riding across the moor. Shl enticed my son to stop and talk with her, es another admirer of hers coming up, my son ana he ' quarrelled over her smiles, and my son returned tl I his mother and sisters, bruised and bleeding; .. covered with dust ' "I don't see how Gwen can be to blame for far' Claxton's quarrels," said Mrs. Quillet. "She is to blame I" declared the bailiff angrg• "What is she to set herself up as a lady? family returned home. My wife and daughtl complained to me, and I took my son to task. Au he told me —told me to my face I that he loved the girl,and that he had decided to make her his wife' He—my son—to marry her! Think of that I" " Gwendoline said that he insulted her."

The bailiff sneered. "He insult her I" he exclaimed. "Why, my girls tell me that she is trying to entrap him into a mar- riage 1 And I believe it. She is poor, homeless, a dependent. She would do anything to enter a family like mine, or any honest family, in spits td her fine education and lady-ways! Now the girl 110 no right here. She is a born outcast. I won't have her here setting traps for my son, or any honest man! I demand that you send her away !" Mrs. Quillet looked blank. "Why, where could I send her ?" she ejaculated- " This is her borne 1" "It is not her home! It is Squire Markham house, and the girl has no right here. Is she a servant? Does she earn her bread? No. She lives in high style, is waited upon, uses the squire's property, and plays lady. She is a swindler, madam, and you have made her so! New she must leave this house at once or I'll write to the squire and tell him of your high handed proceedings here I won't any longer countenance this beggar and out- cast in her swindling existence. Give me your answer. Shall she go—or shall I push this matter to a scandal, and have you and your husband turned out of the house where you have spent your lives Which shall it be ?" He waited for his answer, looking ft-ern• Mrs. Quillet to the girl and back again, feeling hirnsoli master of the situation. (To be continued).

SATURDAY.

At the Saturday sitting of the House of Commons the tlebate on the Address was resumed, Mr. James Lowther In"ing his amendment urging that the IMMIGRATION OF DESTITUTE ALIENS ould be restricted . Mr .GLansroNE,af ter a graceful tribute 12 the late Mr. Jennings, me,nber for Stockport, pressed IT Lowther for a definition of the term " destitute "nen," and asked if he meant that every immigrant who landed on our shores, unless he came with an agreement J,capital in his pocket, was a destitute alien. If they ck at men who came to this country with a capacity :or work and who did not become a burden, they would le at the interests of thousands of labourers exported ally from this country. Was it desirable for a ~..`"llrltry that exported a considerable commodity to put Tcs•traints on the importation of the commodity ? By so p'ing they would be giving a justification to foreign ,2Wers to adopt similar measures. The Government ,7ere making every effort to place the House in a posi- L'lon to judge whether it was expedient to deal with IS question. It would,therefore, be scarcely honest to tee.9ePt the motion; in fact, if they accepted it without „„lug able to arrive at a practical result, they would be ""tY of obtaining popularity under false pretences. pheer other members ha() spoken the House divided, and DT.re were—for Mr.Lowther's amendment, 119 ; against, ; majority against, 115. The Address was agreed to %raid loud Ministerial cheers. kOIiDAY.—INTRODUCTION OF THE HOME RULE BILL. 4 The Reuse of Commons was densely crowded on Mon- -1:113' by members eager to hear Mr. GLADSTONE'S speech introducing the Home Rule Bill. Peers and strangers „4.11 ed the galleries, and over the clock were the PRINCE ~vt WALES and the Duke of YORK. The SPEAKER took the -"air at three o'clo,k, and half an hour afterwards Mr. ?r-AasroNE entered the House amidst enthusiastic cheer- g. laying his Home Rule Bill before the House the "ght hon. gentleman said that in regard to Ireland l'arliainent had to moon BETWEEN AUTONOMY AND COERCION.

'The Coercion to which Ireland had been subjected was Llot compatible with true political stability or true social 'lvilisation, and it was a distinct and violent breach of romise on the faith of which the Union was obtained. • ter showing that until secret voting was established pre was no possibility of learning the wishes of the people, he said that if there was anything in the 6"cat principle of self-government the voice of the Irish roPle and their persistency in the expression of that Dice constituted a great fact in history. The • PROTESTANTS OF IRELAND during the independent Irish Parliament were zealous enthusiastic supporters of Irish nationality, and the ti‘iberal party could not be persuaded that they would t go back again to the sentiments of their ancestors. "ough the principal opposition to Home Rule came from • gland, he reminded the House that the English Parlia- pentary repre.entatives in favour of it had increased ,rom 12-7 in 1686 to 197 nov-, and those against it had ?ecreased from 338 to 268. In the bill he was now Introducing he had endeavoured to closely cohere to tike

)(Aver was given to the Irish Legislature, which would icPsist of a Legislative Council and of a Legislative .75emb1v, to make laws for the peace, order, and good ~..I°Yernnient of Ireland in respect of matters exclusively .rlating to Ireland, and the matters reserved to the nPenal Parliament were all that related to the Crown It''r Regency and Viceroyalty, all that related to peace ,4d war, all that related to defence, all that related to 11:eaties, and all that related to foreign relations and to olguities and titles. The Viceroyalty was to be divested Party character so far as possible, being held for a ;Inn of years, and was to be freed from religious The Legislative Council, which would be a ,t_atection to the minority, would consist of 413 members, uo would be elected for eight years by a constituency teansisting of persons with a value above £2O ; and the ,_egislative Assembly would be left at its present num- :P. Of 103, and would have a term of five years. The vght hon. gentleman proceeded to state the provisions aLor the constitution of the superior courts and the ,PP'Diatnaent of judges, who were to be irremovable. It onat.ProPosed that the Legislative Assembly should meet Waw4egret Tuesday in September. The constabular- al_ t 0 IX withdrawn piecemeal from the local areas on gradual establishment by Irish authorities of a sum- tient new notice force. IRISW REPRESINTATION AT WESTMINSTIR I'rag to be retained, but as according to population Ire- land was only entitled to 90 members in the Imperial Parliament, that was to be the number of Irish repre- sentatives at Westminster. The question what value or Dower their vote was to have would have to be con- aansidered. He had not himself made up his mind !ft the point, but to prevent party intrigue provision lad been made for the limitation ef this voting power. *be Irish members at Westminster were not to vote on 4117 bill or motion expressly confined to Great Britain on all tax not levied in Ireland, or on any vote or appro- ,...Orlation of money otherwise than for Imperial service.
