In the House of Lords the Marquis of SALISBURY drew attention to the action of the Government in hinting to the Ecclesiastical Commissioners that they should deal with the four Welsh dioceses in respect to the creation of new vested interests with full regard to the proposed measure of Disestablishment. His Lordship denounced the conduct of the Government as a" gross and unjusti- fiable transgression of power," and denounced in antici- pation the Horne Rule proposals of the Government.— Lord KIMBERLEY replied to the effect that no instructions had been given to the Ecclesiastical Commissioners that would limit their discretion. WEDNESDAY.
In the ziouse of Commons on Wednesday Mr. LOGAN moved the second reacting, of thelocal Authorities (Vot- ing and qualification) Bi I. the main object of which waste amend the law relating to the

ELECTION OF POOR-LAW GUARDIANS by providing that occupiers only should vote, that all electors (including women) should be eligible for the office, and that election should be lay ballott. Mr. Long thought that if such legislation was considered desirable it should be taken in hand by a responsible Governmetlt. Mr. C. Dilke thought the bill erred rather in not going far enough than in going too far. Mr. J. LOWTHER said he believed the bill was based on unsound prin- ciples, and he hoped the Government would announce that they intended to deal with the matter themselves. Mr. FOWLER said the hands of the Government would be strengthened in their efforts to deal with this ques- tion by the House affirming the principle of the Bill, for the second reading of which he should vote. He hoped that by the inquiries the Royal Commission on the Poor Law were prepared to institute the Government would hereafter be in a position to submit measures adapted to the circumstances of the times. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR, while assenting to the second reading, wished to reserve his right to criticise details. The second reading was agreed to without a division. The second reading of the

div.head: RAILWAY RATES AND CHARGES
div.p: RAILWAY RATES AND CHARGES

(No. 2) Bill was moved by Sir J. WHITBREAD, who said its object was to enable the Board of Trade to say what were fair and reasonable charges in case of dispute. Mr. MIINDRELLA said he could not accept a bill which had not yet been printed, but if by Easter the Railway com- panies had not made a reasonable arrangement with the trader 3 he should be prepared himself to introduce some measure which would effectually deal with the matter. After this statement the Bill was withdrawn.

div.head: TRADE UNION FUNDS. -TORT OBSTRUCTION.
div.p: TRADE UNION FUNDS. -TORT OBSTRUCTION.

On Mr. HOWELL, after half-past five, the limit for opposed business on Wednesday, moving the second reading of a Bill to exempt from intorno tax the invested funds of trade unions applied to provident purposes, Sir M. Hicscs-BEAcn objected, and though Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT said the bill had been approved by the Inland Revenue authorities and Mr. MUNDELLA begged that it might be allowed to proceed, the right hon baronet per- sisted in his objection amidst cries of " Shame," and the Bill had to stand over.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday evening Sir T. ESMONDE called upon Lord Wolmer for an explanation of a statement that the Irish members were being pal d by the parry now in power and that Mr. Gladstone was thus depending on a majority of

FORTY PAID MERCENARIES. Lord WORMER said it was generally admitted that money was no longer forthcoming from Irish or Amtrican sources, and the inference would therefore seem to be irresistible that it was derived from English sources. Mr. SEXTON said the noble Lord had put in circulation an absolute falsehood, and he asked the Speaker whether he ought not to make an instant and absolute apology. The SPEAKER said that as the words were not used with- in the House his jurisdiction did not come in directly, and as the allegation contained in them had been some- what modified by the noble Lord and had been refuted altogether by hon. gentlemen from Ireland he thought the matter should rest there. Lord WOLMER said his intention was to reflect on the Government and not on the Irish members, and he frankly expressed his regret for having used these words. Mr. SEXTON, after describing the noble Lord's withdrawal as niggardly and ungracious, said he had to call attention to the use made of the calumny in that day's " Times "in the course of an article on the payment of members, wherein it des- cribed the Irish members as stipendiary patriots, and he moved that the article was a breach of the privileges of the House. Lord WORKER again rose, and said that after what had occurred he apologised to the Irish party Mr. SEXTON insisted that the question of breach of privi- lege by the" Times "was one for the House to decide, and Mr.J. REDMOND seconded the hon. member's motion. Mr. GLADSTONE was of opinion that the article contained a distinct charge of corruption, and said that if he was asked whether such a charge against any body of members was a breach of privilege he could only give one answer. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR said he must emphati- cally express his firm conviction that not one of the hon. geatlemen referred to in the article was ever bribed or corrupted for his work in that House or took the part he did from any other motive than to promote the good of his country; but he advised the House to be cautious before entering upon an indecorous conflict with the press. Mr. COURTNEY thought it disputable whether a breach of privilege had been committed, and Mr. J. CHAMBERLAIN, while of opinion that there had been a breach of privilege, thought it would be wise not to pro- ceed with the motion. After some further discussion, the motion that the article constituted a gross breach of the privileges of the House was agreed to. THE ORDER OF PROCEDURE. __ . .

Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to Mr. A. J. Balfour, said that on Monday the House would proceed to the appoint- ment of a Chairman of Committees. Then it was pro- posed to introduce the Registration Bill, next the Em- ployers' Liability Bill, and then the Railway Servants' Hours Bill.

div.head: DEBATE ON HOME ROLE:
div.p: THE DEBATE ON HOME ROLE:

The debate on the motion to bring in the Horne Rule Bill was resumed by Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, who said he had never called and never would call the PRIME MINISTER'S proposals anything but repeal of the Union. If we gave the Irish people a Parliament under the peculiar conditions proposed we should give them almost irresistible power of extracting from us any constitutional concessions which would enable them to use their power independently of us more freely than ever. In the present Bill Ulster seemed to have passed entirely out of his mind. The Government did not believe in the resistance of Ulster, but he did. To leave out all mention a that province and to bear in mind at the same time the history of Protestant Ulster was,be thought the most craven insult ever offered by a British Govern- ment to a loyal community. In response to the appeal by Mr. Bryce,that the Unionists would moderate their op- position,the noble Lord declared that no compromise was possible,not even the shade of the shadow of a compromise. Mr. Atherley Jones spoke against the retention of Irish members at Westminster. Mr. Labouchere thought that the Prime Minister had met the difficulties in a most successful manner, and that the bill was a very,good bill as a basis on which to go into Committee. One of the proposals to which he objected was the creation of a second Chamber. The debate was adjourned.

In the House of Lords the Earl of Dunraven asked for the evidence upon which the Government had decided to recommend the issue of a Royal Commission on the land question in Wales. Lord Kimberley said a prima fade case had been made out for the inquiry, and the pro- posal was supported by a great majority of the Welsh members. The Marquis of Salisbury believed that all Mr. Gladstone knew about Welsh affairs came from two noble lords, and if they were wrong the Cabinet would go into a ditch. He asserted that land in England and land in Wales were on all fours, and that Parliament had no right to interfere in contracts between landlord and:tenant.
POINTS OF THE HOME RULE BILL.
A summary of the points of the Home Rule Bill, as set forth in Mr)yGladstone's speech, may be useful to our readers.
THE PREAMBLE. The preamble declares the supreme authority of Parliament to be unimpaired and unrestricted.
THE ENACTING CLAUSES.

The clauses provided for an Irish Legislature, with " power to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Ireland, in respect to matters exclusively relating to Ireland, or some part thereof " ; they settle the constitution of the new Legislature. they expressly reserve certain legislation for the Imperial Parliament : they devolve the powers of the Crown on a Viceroy, ap- pointed for six years, and provide him with an Execu- tive Committee; they reserve a power of veto to him and to the Crown ; they safeguard the interests of the judges and the Royal Irish Constabulary; they provide for the retention of Irish members in Parliament with a limited voting power, and they set forth a scheme for the settlement of the financial relationships of Great Britain and Ireland.
THE NEW LEGISLATURE.

The new Legislature is to consist of two Chambers: (a) The Legislative Council.—This is to be a represen- tative Chamber of 48 members, elected for eight years by :voters (owners or occupiers) with a twenty pound rating qualification, no voter to exercise his franchise in more than one constituency. Its constitution cannot be altered by any Act of the Irish Parliament. In the event of a conflict with the Legislative Assembly, the Bill on which dispute has arisen may be sent up again after two years or after a dissolution, and in the event of the Bill being again refused, it must be then considered and the issue determined by the joint vote of the two Houses.

(b) The Legislative Assembly.—This is to be an assem- bly of 103 members representing the same constituencies 1 and elected in the same way as the present members for 1 Ireland. They must seek re-election before sittina in the Irish Parliament. The duration of this House is only to be five years. After six years it may legislate as to its own numbers, but is bound to have regard to the distribution of population in any Reform Bill which it ' may pan. It will have the control of Money Bills, but

div.head: 111 E TaAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1893.
div.p: 111 E TaAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1893.

these must previously originate with the Viceroy and his Committee. DISABILITIES OF THE IRISH PARLIAMENT. The Acts of the Irish Parliament will only be valid in so far as they are not contrary to Acts of the Imperial Parliament. The t}ew legislature will be incapacitated by the statute from passing Acts injurious to reli2ious freedom or restricting personal liberty. It will have nothing to do with such subjects as the Crown, a Regency, or the Viceroy, peace or war, national defence, treaties, or foreign relations, dignities, cr titles, the law of treason, alienage, trade, or coinage. The land ques- tion is to be reserved to the Imperial Parliametit for three years.
DATE OF MEETING,
The first Tuesday in September, 1894, is the date con- templated for the meeting of the Irish Parliament.
THE VICEROY AND THE VETO:

The Viceroy in future is to be appointed for six years, subject to the revoking power of the Crown, and he is to have an Executive Committee, consisting of members of the Irish Privy Council, on whose advice he will give or withhold his consent to Irish legislation, subject to the instruction of the Sovereign in respect to any par- ticular Bill. He and his Committee alone have the power of appealing to the Privy Council to decide any question arising as to the invalidity of any Act of the Irish Parliament.

to get away, but the tackling of the homesters, if safe, was likewise vigorous. Nevertheless Warrington main- -tamed a footing well in,ide Dewsbliry's quarters'. and relief was only brought about by Bedford baffling Potts, and reaching the Warrington lines again. Bate (Dews- bury) got away, but was q-uickly overhaaled, and then a strong rush by Fair Turner was succeeded by Donohue Berry, and Evans, reaching the home quarters. Another powerful punt by Stadden changed the venue, And Boscow was loudly applauded for a capital save under his posts. Thorniley cleared, and play was at half way when the _ Interval Arrived,

with Dewsbury in a majority by a goal (dropped) and a try. On resuming the play opened in favour of Dews- bury, whose forwards resorted to short rushes, barely allowing the oval to leave the scrimmage. However, when It did become loose, the Bates soon made it warm for the Tykes, and an excellent series of exchanges ter- minated in Potts taking the oval to the line. John Bate got finely away from a pack, and Evans missed a fine chance, Scott eventually kicking dead. Success attended the Warringtonians a minute later, Evans this time making no mistake with a pass from John Bate, Scoring Near the Corner,

Fair Turner making a bold bid for premier honours. Following this came a prolonged raid on the home lines, and the second try was sent up by John Bate, who,with the aid of his companion half, upset an attempt to relieve by Stadden, finally scoring, but in a too difficult position for Potts to improve. Whilst Potts was taking the place an objection was taken against the kick; but the Warringtonians essayed the task, and although Ashton appealed for a second try, the referee turned a deaf ear to all entreaties. Warrington were still two points in arrear, and the drop out saw them attacking as severely as ever. The Dewsbury forwards played a ' vicious game, and after they had by sheer strength re- moved hostilities to half way, a spell of rough forward work commanded attention. Davies was all but in from sne rush, whilst Frank Turner got splendidly away, from a line-out, only to .fmd the• whistle against him. Sharp practice by Warriqgton completely baffled the homesters, and the eccentricities of the two Bates be- , hind the pack in no small measure accounted for the visitors' now marked superiority. Boscow was rarely called upon, and from a line-out Potts took a chance from John Bate, getting over cleverly, but to the sur- prise and evident disgust of the scorer the oval was called back and scrimmaged at the quarter flag. How- ever, the Warringtonians were not daunted by the unjust decisions which awaited their efforts, and a rush in which the whole body of forwards were prominent, resulted in James Bate

Scoring an Unmistakable Try. Potts was entrusted with the easy place, but the attempt proved futile, and the teams restarted on level terms. The last stages of the game were marked by rough for- ward play, the Tykes resorting to tactics unworthy of any organization. Comment is unnecessary on the last portion of the game, and the final result read as a draw, the score reading as—Warrington three tries (six points) to Dewbury a dropped goal and a try (six points). div.head: ZUDGES AND CONSTABULARY._
div.p: ZUDGES AND CONSTABULARY._

The judges are to be irremovable ; and for six years judges will be appointed as at present, the emoluments of any future judge will be fixed by the Irish Parliament to which is thus secured a joint control. The Royal Irish Constabulary are to be gradually transferred into, or replaced by forces under local authorities, bat are meanwhile under the Viceroy's control.

div.head: IRISH MEMBERS IN THE IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IRISH MEMBERS IN THE IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

The number of Irish members in the Imperial Parlia- ment will in future be eighty, and they will not vote on Bills or motions expressly confined to Great Britain, or on any tax not levied in Ireland, or on any vote or ap- propriation of money other than for Imperial services. The provisions regarding them are qualified by the proviso" unless and Until Parliament shall otherwise determine."

div.head: IRISH FINANCE.
div.p: IRISH FINANCE.
By the financial arrangements, the contributifm of Ireland to Imperial purposes is secured out of the Cus- toms Revenue.

div.head: HOME RULE BILL FROM A WELSH POINT OF VIEW.
div.p: THE HOME RULE BILL FROM A WELSH POINT OF VIEW.

Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., Junior Lord of the Treasury and Ministerial Whip, having been asked to give his opinion of the Home Rule Bill in its relatien to Welsh national questions, has replied—" From the point of view of a Federal Home Ruler, no Bill could be introduced which so clearly and unmistakably prepares the way for the extension of the principle of Home Rule to Wales and Scotland. If the Bill is passed, the longest step will have been taken towards what many Welsh Liberals consider, in its issues and consequences, the greatest reform in the Welsh programnae or within the Welsh purview. Every vote, therefore, given for the passing of the Home Rule Bill is a vote given in meaning, and almast in reality, for Welsh nationalistic government. With re- gard to its effect on disestablishment, Mr. Ellis was of opinion that, its first effect was that the momentous re- cognition of the rights and claims of nationality would of itself act as an immense impetus towards the recogni- tion of the Welsh claim for Disestablishment : and that in the coming debates upon the Suspensory Bill the effect of the Home Rule Bill would be perceptibly and con- stantly felt in the debate and the division.

div.head: DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE AND THE HOME RULE BILL.
div.p: THE DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE AND THE HOME RULE BILL.

The Duke of Devonshire, speaking on Tuesday night at a dinner given by the Liberal Union Club to Lord Wolmer, said Mr. Gladstone's second measure of Home Rule failed in every respect to meet almost every one of the objections which they took to the bill of 1886. The only attempt which had been made to meet those I objections had been by proposing to introduce into the Parliamentary system elements which must result in confusion and weakness. The difficulties they felt in regard to the question of the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament had not been met, and the promised special provision for the protection of minorities had not been discovered. The bill was discribed on the previous night as 'one to make better provision for the govern- ment of Ireland, but he should rather describe it as one to create confusion in the government of the United Kingdom. What Ireland most required at the present time was firm, resolute government, resting upon the support of a powerful Imperial Parliament. Whatever might be the fate of the bill in the House of Commons, it would not pass into law in this Parliament. The measure would have to go back to the constituerices again, and when once more they had heard the appeal of Ulster he believed it would be rejected.

div.head: MR. J. b. GILLIAT, M.P., ON THE HOME
div.p: MR. J. b. GILLIAT, M.P., ON THE HOME
RULE BILL.

Speaking at the Garston Conservative Club on Tues- day night, Mr. J. S. Gilliat, M.P. for the Widnes Divi- sion, told the members who had assembled at a smok- ing concert that he was not among those who failed to understand Mr. Gladstone's enigmatic utterances. His Home Rule Bill was the most mischievous Home Rule Bill ever put before a body of Englishmen. There was no protection whatever for minorities, and nothing was done for those loyal Ulstermen who were bearing the brunt of the battle in Ireland. The bill was admirably cooked, but it was one of the worst dishes ever served. The bill must be hurled away. It would probably re- ceive its first reading on Friday, and the great battle would take place on the second reading, after which there would be a long fight in Committee, from which the bill would probably emerge so shorn that its author would not recognise it. Beyond that he declined to pro- phesy. He hoped the Bill would be squashed, but if it went to the Lords it would be thrown out, and then the people would have to decide the question. Whenever that time came and there was a general election, they would find him perfectly ready ,to fight their battle. (Applause.) --

div.head: "FREAK OF NATURE."
div.p: A "FREAK OF NATURE."

A freak of nature even more remarkable than that of the Siamese Twins is reported from Nanking, where a Kiansi man has two sons, aged about eight, who are joined together by an "arm-like piece of flesh," about the size of a man's arm, in such wise that they stand, not side by side but face to face. A writer, who has axamined them, states that when they walked they had to move sideways, or shoulders first, " like the peregrin- ations of a crab." Nor did there seem to be any diffi- culty for one to sit while the other stood. Another curious incident was that the twins never fell asleep at the same time, for while one was asleep the other was sure to be awake. The twins have had audiences of all the authorities at Nanking, crowds collecting aronnd them whenever they went about the streets with their father.

RUGBY. LANCASHIRE CUP COMPETITION. WARRINGTON v. TYLDESLEY.

With both sides adopting the Welsh system of four three-quarters for this return engagement, visitors to Wllderspool on Saturday had an opportunity of adjudi- cating on the subject which has claimed attention throughout the present season since Wales defeated England. Many have argued in favour of the Taffys' idea, but the general verdict of Saturday's engagement was distinctly against it, the wing three-quarters, especially in the second half, receiving but scant atten- tion. As stated, the match was the return fixture, and there would be considerably over 4,000 present, when hostilities were commenced. Nevins and Heesom were away from the home side, the latter not having recov- ered from the injury sustained in the Oldham match. Winning the toss, the visitors defended the pavilion goal, and _

Turner Kicked Off with almost a gale against him and the sun in his eyes. His kick-off was followed by P. R. Lawless making further headway by a sort of hurdle :race, and the game was taken to Tyldeslny quarter-flag. A couple of kicks by Bell and Shaw were sufficient to land the oval at the opposite.end, and Boscow was busily employed, a good screw landing his aide at half-way. Another kick by Boscow and Wilson at fault, and the game was favouring Warrington, when Shaw and Taylor stepped into the breach and forced the homesters to retire back to their own territory. Turner got away from a line- out and gained considerable ground with one rush, whilst Ashton and Donohue dribbled well until foiled by W. Berry. The latter again demonstrated himself a monsent later, but his kick being too strong, Boscow allowed the get minor to go up in favour of Tyldesley. The game remained interesting on Turner's drop-out, and some clever work by Jeley, Higham, and Ashton, served as relief, but the Bates foiling the Berm James Bate got away,and Tyldesley now had a spell of defence. A pass from Smith to Bell saw the latter running well until he fell into the clutches of P. R. Lawless, and although Evans temporarily staved off the invasion, another bout of judicious kicking by Shaw, Taylor, and Framley was met in brilliant style by Boscow and Web- ster. The latter put the finishing touch to some passing by the Bates, whilst W. Berry being penalized for a gross infringement, Turner's kick was well followed up by Ashton, Edwards, and Glover, and Warrington again had the better of the deal. A good deal of fluctuating play followed,but the bomesters were looking dangerous when the whistle sounded the interval. With the Score Sheet Blank.

On re-starting the wind bad considerably, but the general estimation arrived at was that the locals would win easily. However, a surprise was in store, and directly after the kick Off the Tyldesley forwards rushed down the open, and overcoming opposition, a minor was granted in the first minute. Webster was instrumental in giving his side their first footing in Tyldesley territory, and J. Lawless putting in a finished bit of play, J. Berry (Warrington) charged a kick of W. Berry, and the homesters looked certain scorers until Wilson gathered well and punted out of danger. A drop by Boscow sent up Warrington's second minor, and although Fearnley ran well on the drop-out, the effort was more than neutralized when Turner, Edwards, and I Evans rushed the oval back to the Tyldesley lines,Wilson again saying. A long dribble by Tinker brought about a permanent attack on the home goal, and after W. Berry had made strenuous efforts to get in, he at one essay threw from almost one touch line to the other, with the result that J. Fearnley Scored a Somewhat Easy Try, which proved to be the winning point of the game. With Shaw's failure at goal Warrington attacked, but the opposing forwards were decidedly masters of the situa- tion, and although J. Lawless gathered well and looked dangerous, he found the opposition a trifle too strong. Ashton and Turner led to the line, but it was a futile essay, and the remainder of the play being of a forward nature comment is unnecessary, and in the end War- rington were defeated by a try and three minors to four minors.

Teams :—Warrington: J. Boscow. back ;H. Webs- ter, J. Lawless, J. W. Evans, and P. R. Lawless, three- quarters ; John Bate and James Bate, half-backs; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, J. Jolley, W. Glover, T. Donohue, J. Berry, H. Edwards, and J. Higham, forwards. Tyldesley : S. Wilson, back ;J. Fearnley, F. Shaw, H. Bell, and H. Taylor, three-quarters; W. Berry and J. Berry, half backs; G. Woodward, W. Sutcliffe, J. Tinker, A. Smith, W. Whitehead, J. Fell, W. Roberts, and J. Worthington, forwards. Referee, Mr. E. Seddon Broughton. . WARRINGTON v. DEWSBURY.

With an excellent combined team the Warringtonians journeyed to Dewsbury on Tuesday morning to play off their return fixture with the well-known Yorkshire or- ganization. Crown Flatts was in excellent condition, and Shrove Tuesday being a recognized holiday with the Tykes, there was an attendance of close on 4,000. The iiomesters bad a strong team up, their backs including J. P. Bate, who had recently been granted his reinstate- ment by the Yorkshire Committee. A gale was blowing from goal to goal, and winning the toss Stadden took advantage of the elements. Frank Turner's rick Off was followed by some smart play of the visiting for- wards, notably- Higharn Fair Turner, and Davies, and Warrington for a time had the better of the deal, until Bate (Dewsbury) relieved with a tall punt, and Boscow missing his footing the ball was taken over, but glaring off-side play by Jackson and Gee ruled the oval still at the Dewsbury, quarters. Better luck attended an effort by Stadden and Bedford, and Boscow had all his work cut out to keep his lines intact. A daring save by the Warrington castodian and kicks by Evans and Lawless staved off the invasion, whilst some excellent passing by the two Bates nonplussed the Tykes and play again ruled at the half-way flag. Eventually the homesters got away in a body, and Boscow' s kick being carried back over the line by the wind, Oldroyd Scored la lucky try at the corner, which Scott failed to improve upon. Minors followed to the credit of Dewsbury, and then James Bate baffled Stadden, and Frank Turner and Davies taking up the running, Warrington again reached the home quarters. Scott cleared, and in one essay reachee'. the Warrington lines. A sequence of passes by the Bates and Lawless gained tem/wary relief, but another attempt saw Lawless punting to Scott, who made his mark near the half-way, and taking the drop he succeeded in registering the premier point. Follow- ing this came some all-round excellent form by the Lancashire men, Thorniley and Berry leading the way. The Bates passed accurately, and repeatedly befooled the Dewsburylhalf-backs. Evans made strenuous efforts

div.head: Defence and Attack
div.p: Defence and Attack

the Warringtonians were the smarter team, and this is in no small measure due to the brilliant play of both John and James Bate. The manner in which they over- played Stadden and Jackson, the Dewsbury half backs, caused surprise amongst the Pical enthusiasts. Boscow played a sound game, and whilst Evans was the most effective of the three-quarters, Lawless was a finished centre, and Potts, indeed, was not found wanting. The forwords, too, worked hard, and, be it said to their credit, their unflagging energy came at a time when required.

div.head: Teams:
div.p: Teams:

Warrington : Boscow, back ; Evans, Lawless, and Potts. three-quarter backs; John Bate and James Bate, half- backs; 11. Ashton, Fair. Turner, Donohue, Berry, Higham, Davies, Thorniley, Frank Turner, and Eden, forwards. Dewsbury: Scott, back ; Dedford, J. P. Bate and Goldthorpe, three-quarter backs ; Stadden and Jackson, half backs; Garforth, Kenworthy, Randall, Gee, Abel, Hodgson, Grundill, Oldroyd, and Bottomley, forwards.

WARRINGTON" A" v. TYLDESLEY "A."—At Tyldesley. Warrington started against a strong wind, Eden being the means of his side gaining a footing inside the home 25. A series of scrimmages was followed by Tyldesley rushing to the centre line, whence Smith, Lally, and Potts transferred the warfare to near their opponents' goal. Further transfers amongst the visiting backs ended in the Warrington man being robbed of the leather, and away Tyldesley rushed right to the other end, Massey kicking dead in the nick of time. Aided by the powerful breeze, the home time pressed, but when they tried the passing system amongst their four three- quarters, ground was lost and any impending danger averted. Here Lally shot away, passing to Potts, who ran down the centre and threw to Massey. This player put on top speed, and ropnding Cottam screwed splen- didly across, Teare having little difficulty in compl6ting a grandly-earned try. From the drop out the ,ball was driven in the loose to the Warrington quarter, where after acme scrimmage work a few kick was granted to Tyldesley. The kick in the dangerous position was charged, but a shady trick of the home team enabled Miller to score and Duckworth to kick a goal. With this lead the" Bongers " played up with renewed vigour, showing neat passing, but Ashurst on one occasion cleared finely, half time shortly afterwards being declared. Bradbury, Davies, Flampson, and Bailey ,Iroye their antagonists back to their lines, Lally, from a pass by Smith, ran to the quarter flag, a long kick rolling dead. Warrington now had a turn of attacking, Teare, Monks and Barratt showing up prominently, and from a kick by a Tyldesley back Massey scored near touch. Potts took the place, and by a magnificent kick sent the ball flying over the bar. The game, which had been anything but pleasant, now degenerated consider- ably, the offside tactics and reprehensible tricks adopted by the home team making the contest most disagreeable to watch. Warrington still attacked strongly, Moly- neaux, Bradbury, Davies, and Bailey being notable, and Lally, scooping up the ball, ran:in, but, unfortunately, lost possession, a minor being allowed, a couple more being immediately conceded. Then Tvldesley had a look in, but were penalized for offside %alien dangerous, and the warfare taken to the other end of the field, Potts dropping a capital goal. Nothing more was obtained, Warrington winning by 2-1-5 to 1-0-1. RUNCORN V. SALE.—At Runcorn, before a large atten- dance. Both teams were well represented. After some fluctuating play Taylor scored for Runcorn, but Crompton failed at the place. After an attack by Sale, Farmer scored again, Crompton again failing. Shortly afterwards Kingston got over without difficulty, but again the place kick failed. At half-time, Runcorn led by three tries to nil. In the second half Runcorn had all the hest of the game, and finally won by 2 goals and three trif s to nil. RUNCORN FIORNETS V. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH " A " TEAK.—The Hornets jurneyed to Warrington on Saturday to play the return fixture with the above- named club. As the Church first team had no match, it was evident that the Hornets would have a good strong team to face. After 70 minutes hard play the game ended in a draw, neither side scoring. The Hor- nets have played 22 matches, and have won 18, lost four, and drawn two, a record which many a junior club would be proud of. WIDNES V. DUICINVIELD.—At Widnes. Barber kicked

off for Widnos, who led at the interval by a try to nothing. In the second half Dukinfield were seldom over the centre line, and Clarke, Hughes, Johnson, and Wynne scored tries. Brennan dropped a goal, and Barber placed three goals, Result—Widnes, 4 goals and 2 tries t 23 points) ; Dukinfield, nil.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB V. LANCASHIRE INDEPEN- DENT COLLEGE.—These teams met on the Cricket ground on Saturday. The Cricket Club kicked off against a strong wind, and the college began to press at once, their quick passing completely nonplussing the home halves. However, the Cricket Club full backs played an excellent game and prevented their scoring. At lenghth the Cricket Club got away and Fenelly with a very lucky shot opened the score for the Cricket Club. Soon afterwards the Cricket Club, having all the best of the luck, scored again, Isherwood giving the finishing touch. The game stood at half time 2to nil in favour of the Cricket Club. The second half was exactly like the first, the visitors passing again and again, but their shooting was bad and they only scored once, while Hoare got a third goal for the Cricket Club, the game ending in a victory of 3-1. for the home team. Hannah and Francomb at full back and Forrest at goal played remarkably well for the Cricket Club. Cricket Club team—Goal: Forrest; full backs, S. Francomb, W. Hannah ; half backs, F. Williamson, L. Smith, and R. E. Kenyon ; forwards, W. H. Reid, Fenelly, laherweod, A. R. floare, and G, Williamson. Waratmorox v. ST. HELENS JUNCTION.—The above fixture was played on the Warrington ground at Arpley on Saturday. A certain amount of interest was cen- tred in the match as the visitors had on two occasions berten the St. Elphin's Club both at home and away. Up to half time the game was steadily contested, the homesters, however, having the lead from a goal shot by Radford. During the second half of the game the homesters had en repeated occasions very hard lines in not scoring, and played a far better game than their opponents. The score when time was called wiz War- rington, one goal ; St. Helens, nil. WARRINGTON RICKNRI7E V. WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCSIOOL.—PIayed on Saturday on the School ground. Warrington played during the first half with the wind in their favour and put on a couple of goals, while the School team were nnable to score. The second half was evenly played, and nothing further was scored, the re- sult being Warrington 2 goals, School nil.
" OWD MOLLY CUCKOO" AND HER " OWD HARRY !"

Dame Molly wur a rum owd lass, Ez ever' ticked a word ; " But hoo wur streyght, an' yo' cud trust Her very leetest word. To say that hoo wur scrumshus, lads, Wur stretchin it; but then Wot cud a gradely judge expect, Fro such a hawful sken ? Aw fancy aw con see her neaw, On that haul oppen't door, Ez hoo looked reet an' lift at oncet, Fer owt that dropt on th' door; Then beaut her bonnet hoo'd rush off, Armed wi' her rake an' shool ; He trade, ez hoo took care to tell, Required no other tool. But wo betide the sowl that stole A single eaunce i' weight; They'd oather ha' to give it up, Er else turn eaut to feyght ! Moll wuz ez brave ez hoo wur feaw, An' that's not sayin' mitch ; But if hard wark deserted a turn, Hoo owt to ha' deed rich. Owd Harry, he wur th' husband, but He never made his claim; He thowt that quietness wur th' best, An' boss'd it but i' name. Eh, lads! aw shud ha' liket to see That good owd cupple'wed ; Not one streyght eye amung aw four— Not one r oather yed ! It must ha' put —afoor they'd done— That parson in a funk; An' aw shud not ha' bin surprised If he'd begun t' feel drunk! But still, a honester Coved pair N e'er walked eaur village street; An' whether they seed streyght er not, Aw hope they're neaw aw reet ! div.head: Rose Bonk, Feb. 17, 1893.
div.p: Rose Bonk, Feb. 17, 1893.
THE ADOPTION OF CHILDREN.
SHOCKING REVELATIONS.

On Thursday, at the Local Board Office, Kensal Rise, London, an inquiry was held into the circumstances attending the death of a child named Albert Victor Weston, aged about nine weeks, of unknown parentage, who died on January 29. From the evidence of Mrs. Ellen Barnard, of 6, Beethoven-street, Queen's Park, it appeared that in consequence to an advertisement in a Sunday paper she wrote to " Mrs. Weston," whom she subsequently met at Victoria Station, and received the child. The arrangement was £2 down, and more later. The woman told witness that the child was the son of her daughter, a single woman. Witness fed it on milk, , oatmeal, and barley water, but it did not thrive, and died on the 29th ult. Witness had had other children to nurse, but they had not died. She admittea having gone under different names. A doctor stated that a post-mortem examination revealed that there was not a particle of fat on the body, which only weighed gib., the average being Vb. The actual cause of death was practically starvation, through want of proper food.— Sarah Baker, otherwise Weston, the wife of John Baker, a railway porter, residing at 10, Willow Walk, Bermond- sey, said she had lived there ten years. She took in ladies to nurse. The ladies gave what name they liked. All advertisements for nursing came to her private address, directed to Mrs. Beta. The advertisements offering children for adoption were paid for by the mothers themselves.—The jury, after a short consulta- tion, returned a verdict of "Manslaughter against Ellen Barnard." They considered that Mrs. Baker was morally more guilty than Ellen Barnard, and requested the coroner to severely censure her.

div.head: COMING COAL CRISIS.
div.p: THE COMING COAL CRISIS.

Mr. Samuel Woods, M.P., in the course of an inter- view with a representative of the " West minister Gazette " says :—We consider there is no justification whatever for a reduction in wages. Fer a long time the leaders of the Miners' Federation have held the opinion that the laws of political economy, as they are com- monly understood, are not just in their operation to- wards the working classes, consequently, after ex- tended experience and much observation, we have ar- rived at the conclusion that the basis of our action should be the doctrine of political humanity. We hold tba principle most tenaciously that working-men especi- ally in dangerous callings, should be entitled at least to a reasonable living for the work they perform. We are also convinced that there is no depression in the trade, because we find from the returns that within the last five years the annual production has increased by over 25,000,000 tons. Therefore, taking into consideration both the prices ruling and the volume of trade we con- sider the position taken up by the Miners' Federation to be impregnable. Continuing, the hon. gentleman said the leaders of the Federation strongly desired to implrss upon the public the necessity of disregarding any scare which the middlemen may try to create in order to fleece them by raising the price of coal as was the case twelve months ago. There should be no alarm in the public mind, at least until the decision of the Conference is fully known, because by their contracts the mew must give 14 days' notice during which period consumers would have plenty of opportunity for laying in their stocks.
TRADES UNIONISTS AND THE COTTON TRADE DISTRESS.

The pitiable condition to which cardroora hands have been reduced through the present dispute is rousing the practical sympathy of the Trades Unionists of the coun- try. The Amalgamated Engineers have decided upon a levy of sixpence per member, which will realise about 1.,300, and other sections of the trades unionists are similarly bestirring themselves on bebalf of the suffering factory hands.

div.head: RIOTOUS PROCEEDINGS AT A POLITICAL MEETING.
div.p: RIOTOUS PROCEEDINGS AT A POLITICAL MEETING.

On Wednesday night a meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Mclnnes, the Oladstonian candi- date, was held at Rexham. The principal speaker was to have been Dr. R. Spence Watson, president of the National Liberal Federation, and solicitor for the petitioners in the recent trial. A disturbance had been expected, and a number of miners marched from Mickley and Prudhoe to attend the meeting. Fhe proceedings were fairly orderly until Dr. Watson rose to speak, when loud yells and hisses came from various parts of the hall. The Chairman endeavoured in vain to maintain order, and the pitmen interfered. The only result was extra disorder and fights, which spread to all parts of the meeting. Pugilistic encoun- ters took place on all sides, and though the meeting was abandoned ,the fight continued.many ugly wounds being received by the supporters of both candidates. The hall was finally cleared, but there was great excite- ment in the town. The polling took place yesterday.

div.head: SHOCKING WIFE MURDER.
div.p: SHOCKING WIFE MURDER.
DESPERATE STRUGGLE.

A terrible tragedy, says the Press Association's Shef- field correspondent, was enacted ma Thursday morning, at Woodhouse Mill,five miles from Sheffield. A trammer named Edward Heeming at about three o'clock cut his young wife's throat in so terrible a manner that she died almost immediately. The pair had quarrelled frequently,Heeming having accused his wife of unfaith- fulness and extravagance. Several lodgers were aroused by the woman's screams, lout Eleeming shouted that all was right. Another account says that Thursday was the woman's List birthday. Her throat was cut and her head nearly severed, and her forehead battered in. There must have been a tecrible struggle, as several of the woman's fingers were nearly cut off ,and all the furni- ture in the room bespattered with blood. A razor, axe, and pair of clogs were discovered in the fire. The hus- band has disappeared.

div.head: DOUGLAS SENSATION.
div.p: THE DOUGLAS SENSATION.

A case of great interest came before the Deemster'fi Court at Douglas on Monday. which arose out of pro- ceedings for alleged assault which came before the court at Birmingham a few weeks ago, and were detailed at the time. £2OO damages were granted against 'rhos. Harris, a retired gentleman, formerly a wine and spirit Imerchant, for an assault of an extraordinary character I alleged to have been committed upon Rose Morgan, at Douglas, at the defendant's own house at the Isle of Man last summer. The suit now brought was that of Rose Morgan, by Charles Morgan, her nearest friend, against I Thomas Harris, the defendant in the suit at Birming- ham. It was to recover £221 19s. 4d., the amount of 'the Birmingham judgment, including costs. The judg- ment is dated the 27th ult.—Mr. Ring, on behalf of the defendant, promised to put in a defence ; and the case which has aroused the greatest interest, was ad] • ourned for a fortnight.

div.p: ture consist of two Houses, both of which are to be elective. What may be spoken of as the Upper Chamber—the Legislative Council—will be com- posed of forty-eight members elected by rate- payers with a twenty Pounds qualification; the " Lower " Chamber will comprise 103 members elected as members of Parliament are now elected. From a Radical or a democratic poict of view, there are, undoubtedly, objections to be urged against an" Upper" House elected upon a twenty Pound franchise, but it is in every way preferable to the analogous contrivance of 1886. It is for example, an elective body, and there is in it no re- cognition of the hereditary privileges of peers to govern. In the practical work of framing his Bill Mr. GLADSTONE could not entirely ignore, however Much he might dissent from, the persistent asser- tions of the ITnionists that an Irish legislature Would at once take in hand the spolia- tion of the propertied classes. This cry Will now lose all its speciousness. If the Unionists of Ireland embrace, as they say they tlot at least three-fourths of the wealth of that country they will be in a position to mould to their own liking a chamber which is elected upon a twenty-pound franchise. At the same time the Legislative Council or the " Upper " House will not be in a position to obstruct popular measures to an unlimited extent. It is true that bills that are passed by the Assembly, or Lower Chamber, will have to pass it too, but the possibility of a deadlock is foreseen and provided for. When a till has been passed by the Assembly and rejected bY the Legislative Council the former body may again send it up either after a general elec- ti°ll or the lapse of two years, and if it be again Nected the two bodies will then have to sit to- gether as a united Legislature and vote upon the In that event the Assembly, which is the luore numerous body,will generally secure its ends, though probably not with out more or less of that ecenprornise which seems essential to the smooth werkiug of Parliamentary machinery. Another !dal departure from the model of 1886 is found in the retention in the Imperial Parliament of the Irish members, whose numbers Will, however, be reduced from 103 to 80, which is about the representation Ireland is entitled to On the score of population. It was the clause excluding the Irish 'members which had much to do with wrecking the earlier Homo Rule Bill; and, notwithstanding several obvious difficultiew in the Way of retaining them, there can be little doubt that the g-overunlolit ChOS the line of least resist- Moe hi deciding to do so. :13 AtFouu was the first of the " heavy guns" On the Opposition benches to attack the Bill, and it must at once be said that his criticisms were of the pettifogging order. In the very opening of his speech Mr. GLADSTONE haq referred in eloquent and impressive language to what may be described as the governing factor in the Irish question. llns is, that Parliament has to choose between autonomy and coercion. There is no middle "I's° ; and, added Mr. GLADSTONE, "if there is anythiug in the great principle of self-govern- raent the voice of the Irish people and their Persistency in the expression of that voice, consti- statute m Ntv.hich a grelt fact in history." The Irish de- and, and persist in demanding, in the method has been provided for them by the constitu- of this country, that the right to control toThr Own domestic affairs should be restored 'll Mr. GLADSTONE seeks to comply with that reeq.uest in a manner which, as he contends, n harmony t with the best interests of the E.mpire, and he paints out that the only altorna- ive to complying with that request is to govern the Irish by coercion as a subject and an alien People. What then,is the position taken up by the Opposition so far as Mr. BA LOUR can be regard- ed as their spnkesman ? Mr. BALFOUR does not attempt to point out a third alternative, nor does he, as the logic of his position demands, seek to justify a system of perpetual coercion. He con- tents himself almost entirely with retailing a num- ber of minor difficulties which will be encountered in carrying out Mr. GLADSTONE'S plan, such diffi- culties, for instance, as have relation to the treat- tent of civil servants, the mapping out of Ireland Into constituencies, the appointment of judges, and the contributions of Ireland to the Imperial ,i(;hequer. On the broad principles which are involved he has little or nothing to say, and this, iii itself, is surely an augury: of the success of the tiorne Rule Bill,for no great act of political justice long be withheld when its most pro- nounced and ablest opponents can advance no Stronger objections than the difficulties incident to carrying out what are, after all, mere details of adininistration.
Lancashire AN inquiry into the political _coin-

County plexion of the occupants of our i Magistrates. County Bench reveals some strik- N facts. There are some 740 individuals enjoy- the honourable distinction in question, of Iyhllool no fewer than 522 re known Tories or Liberal unienizts and only 142 are believed to be Liberals. eollling to our own neighbourhood we find that Zit of a total of 25 gentlemen who comprise the ,xnrarrington Petty Sessional Bench, there are 18 ries, three Liberal Unionists, and only four 'Liberals. This condition of affairs naturally sug- 14e8tS an inquiry into its cause. The most ardent 'not to say stupid—Tory would not for a 41°/nent claim that the relative numbers of the two political parties in Lancashire would justify elich a flagrant misuse of patronage as these facts disclose. The necessary brains and the capability t° administer justice are certainly not pre- erainently a characteristic of the Tory party. The fttise appears even worse when we find that since Zue Year 1886 only 35 Liberal county magistrates "4.e.va been appointed as against 177 Tories. What "hen is the explanation of this most unjust and Ilowise anomaly? It seems that some 17 years ago,the Crown co-opted upon the Lord Lieutenant of Le county for the time being the power of tecomnneneling fit and proper persons for appoint- ee „ent• The Lord Lieutenart holds his office for 'Be term of his natural life. When the present holder of this office (Lon]) SEFTON) was appointed he Was a "Whig," but he never would nominate 411 Y gentleman for the position of County Magis- trate whose name had not been already approved of by the sitting justices ; as a result during th e tinle that a Liberal administration was in office occasionally a Liberal was "sandwiched" between a couple of Tories and was duly appointed, but Whenever the Tory party held the reins of Gov- ernment, a Liberal had no chance. No wonder then that the Liberals of Lancashire of all ranks 4re thoroughly disgusted and determined that the Present condition of things shall not be tolerated )314.114. longer. They also feel that the qualifica- "l°ns for the office of County Justice (which are 4...nother evidence of the manner in which our :e„islature has been "worked "in tho interest of the" aristocratic" classes) shall not be allowed to _°Perate against the selection of suitable men. The party of " privelege " had already scented dan-

div.p: ger and has besought the Chancellor of the Duchy not to make any alteration in the present method of appointment, protesting meanwhile that everything is perfectly satisfac- tory. How these worthy men had the ineffable " cheek" to so approach Mr. BRYCE with such statements, passes our comprehension, but the Tory party sticks at nothing when its interests appear to be jeopardised. However, the Liberals of the county have not been slow to follow up the matter, and in an interview with Mr. BRYCE a few days ago they were able to produce such a case as elicited from him, not merely an expression of opinion favourable to the views of this second de- putation, but an avowal of a determination to redress the present d iscreditable monopoly at an early date. We hope it will be our privilege to see very shortly a large accession to the County Bench of capable Liberals of all grades of social position, including a satisfactory proportion of working-men.

THE Nationalist members scored Palrliamentary heavily in the House of Com- mons on Thursday evening. Lord WornEn, the Liberal Unionist "Whip," appears to be one of those ill-mannered sprigs of the aris- tocracy who evidently think that they should be allowed to utter with impunity any kind of mean and baseless libel upon Irish Nationalists. In the particular instance which was alluded to on Thurs- day evening he found to his sorrow that he had gone a step too far. After partaking of a banquet on Tuesday evening he had declared in a speech to the effect that the Irish Party included about forty "paid mercenaries," the payment being re- ceived from the Liberal Party. When called to task in the House of Commons for this indecent allegation, Lord WOLMER in an offensive and perky manner declared that he would withdraw it and express his regret if he was assured the "state- ment had no foundation." This, however, did not end the matter, and after an excited discussion in the course of which Lord WOLMER was thrown over by his own leaders, and quietly but severely castigated by Mr. GLADSTONE, the indiscreet lord- ling was glad to withdraw from his untenable posi- tion upon any terms. Pushing their advantage the Irish members indicted their old enemy "The Times" which had commented upon Lord WoL- MER'S unhappy speech in the strain which was so familiar during the Pigot period, and, in the end, the House of Commons unanimously passed a motion, proposed by Mr. SEXTON, that the newspaper referred to had been guilty of a gross and scandalous abuse of the privileges of the House. Time is, clearly, bring- ing its revenges. Thursday's sitting was no- table and interesting from another cause, for after the lapse of two years, and after having travelled in South Africa and had adventures with lions and other wild animals, Lord Randolph CHURCHILL again raised up his voice in the House of Commons. He re-opened the debate on the Home Rule Bill, and, as was to be expected, spoke adversely of Mr. GLADsToNE'S proposals. He had a splendid v.udienc:, the House being almost as crowded as on Monday, but his speech was, from the point of view of his friends, " flat and unprofitable." There is •a concensus of opinion that the noble lord has lost almost all his old sprightliness and power in debate, while his ner- vousness and appearance of physical debility were almost painful to witness. It is conceded that he did nothing to weaken the, position of the Home Rule Bill,

The Mr. STUART BENDEL, M.P., has Enfranehiseneet obtained the first place next of Chapels. Wednesday for the second read- ing of the Places of Worship Enfranchisement Bill. This is a measure which affects to an im- portant extent many Non-conformist bodies in different parts of the country. It is said, for in- stance, that half the chapels in Carnarvonshire aro built on land which is held by a leasehold tenure. In one place in Merionethshire —Blae- nau Festiniog—there are no fewer than seventeen leasehold chapels which cost £37,000, built on lease of sixty years or less, which the landlords can appropriate or compel the congregations to re-purchase as soon as the term expires. That some landlords take the fullest advantage of all that the law allows there is abundant evidence to show. It is said that within the last half-century at least fifty Congregational chapels have ceased to exist, and that there are even yet a consider- able number of them built upon leasehold tenure whose doom is inevitable unless the sites are enfranchished. What used to be known as the Surrey Chapel is now a ware- house for agricultural implements, and the Finsbury Chapel is about to be demolished. "In Sheffield, there is," we are further told, "a Wes- leyan Chapel of which the Duke of Norfolk re- cently offered to grant a renewed lease, provided the people surrendered the old one fourteen years before it expired, and at once began to pay a ground rent of £lOO a year instead of £8 I6s. At Newport (Mon.) the trustees of a Wesleyan Chapel, with twenty-three years cf the term un- expired, on asking for a renewal, were told that they must surrender the old lease, and at once be- gin to pay £lOO a year ground rent instead of £8 4s. At Toxteth (Liverpool), a large Baptist Chapel was built twenty years ago on a lease of seventy-five years, at a ground rent of £4B per annum. Recently the congregation approached the peer who Owns the site with the object of purchasing the freehold, but were curtly told that no such proposal could be entertained." The Bill of which Mr. BENDEL has charge has already passed a second reading in two different Sessions of Parliament; it is to be hoped that it may now
not only pass its second reading, but also all the subsequent stages necessary to make it an Act of Parliament.

At the usual weekly meeting of the Warrington Debating Society, held on Thursday evening. Mr. W. J. Horton read a paper upon "Forward Move- ments—Religious and Social. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. Hulse and those taking part in debate were :—Messrs. A:Bennett, Jno. Gandy, Hall, Ains- cough, and the Chairman. The object of the paper seemed to be to point out that social progression was only sound and true when accompanied by re- ligious motives. ARR/NGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL. At a meeting of the governors of the Warrinaton Grammar School, held on Monday, the Right Hon. Viscount Cross in the chair,the following resolution was passed :—"Resolved,that the governors approve of the proposal of the head master to have a pre- paratory form in the school for boys from 8 to 12 years of age, at a fee of £2 a term, which is the minimum fee allowed by the scheme." The follow- ing have been elected to vacancies on the govern- ing body :—Major Picktnere, J.P., Charles White, Esq., J.P., and the Rev. Richard Greenall.

WESTON BIBLE AND MIITBAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. On Monday night last, in the WesleYan Schoolroran, the Rev. D. W. Arrowsmith gave a lecture entitled " Re- flections on Luther's Work." Mr. P. IL Matthews occu- pied the chair.
A YOUNG THIEF AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday at Runcorn Police Court, Wm. White, aged 12 years, of 29, Bridgewater.st., pleaded guilty to stealing a pair of boors, value 64., from the shop of Thomas Sharrock, High-st. He was sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod.

WIDNES C.E.T.S. In aid of the funds of this temperance organization, special sermons were preached on Sunday. In the morn- ing the Rev. Dr. Oliver D.D., vicar of Glasgow, occupied the pulpit at the Parish Church, and in the evenings the Rev. G. H. Spooner, M.A., rector of Woolton, preached at St. Pauls.

THE RUNCORN STABBING CASE. At Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr. James Handley and Mr. G. L. Davies, Thos. Fisher was again brought up charged with stabbing Arthur Royle. —Superintendent Atherton said the injured boy would not be able to appear for some weeks yet, and the pris- oner was again remanded.

PRESENTATION TO A RIINCORN FOOTBALLER. Mr. J. Fisher, captain of Runcorn Association Foot- ball Club, left the town at the beginning of the week for the purpose of continuing his professional studiss in Manchester. As a token of their appreciation of his services to the club, and of their good wishes for his future welfare, the members have presented him with a case of handsome pipes. . .

MUTILATED By A DYNAMITE FUSS AT WESTON. John Thomas Scott, aged 14 years, of Pritchard's-row, Weston, met with a fearful accident on Saturday night at his father's Louise, by the explosion of a dynamite fuse. The by held the fuse in his left hand, while he lighted it with a match held in his right hand. Immedi- ately the fuse exploded with a loud report. and shattered the thumb and two first fingers.of his left hand. P.C. Penfield rendered first aid and afterwards Dr MacKenzie
dressed the wounded hand. The boy states that he
- picked up the fuse in Weston Quarries.

If you want a lucky wedding ring go to 51, HIGII-ST.,Whet• you will get a present with it.—Advt. Tint RESPONSIBILITIES OF TRADESMEN. At Runcorn County Court on Tuesday before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, Messrs. Partington and Lancaster, grocers, High-st., Runcorn, sued William Goodwin, a Ship Canal ganger. residing at the Ship Canal Huts, Weston Point, for £69s. 9d., the value of goods supplied. The defendant said he was separated from his wife, but previously his wife had kept lodgers and she had obtained creditin her own name, and had paid the weekly bills herself. He had never instructed the plaintiffs to give credit to his wife, or to the woman who was now living with him as his wife, and who, it was alleged, had ob- tained the goods sued for.—The Judge said the responsi- bility rested upon tradesmen not to supply goods to women without the consent of their husbands,and in that ease he was not satisfied that the consent had been given. A verdict would, therefore, be entered for the defendant. JOSEPH PRITCHARD-S sale shop is 51,Hign-st., ma workshop 4, Bridge-st.—Advt.

ALLEGED ROEBEEY WITH VIOLENCE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Peter Conno- ley, aged 18 years, of 6, Caroline-st., was charged with committing highway robbery with violence. Catherine Cassidy, 13 years of age, whose home is in Caroline-st., said about six o'clock on the previous evening her mother sent her with a wheelbarrow for some firewood. When she was passing along Lacey-at., the prisoner came up to her and struck her a blow on the mouth, causing her to fall down. The blow made her nose bleed. While she was on the ground the prisoner took the sixpenny piece, which she was carrying in her hand, forcibly from her, and afterwards ran a.crcss some waste land: Some hours later the prisoner was arrested, and in reply to the charge, admitted that he knocked the girl down, but denied robbing her.-41e was committed to the Liverpool Assizes for trhil. div.head: ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN.

As will be seen from an announcement the Runcorn Branch of the St. John's Ambulance Association will commence classes in St. John's School, on Thursday next, and ladies and gentlemen wishful to join would do would do well to make early application. Dr. McDougall, who has been so successful in the past, will again conduct the classes. At the conclusion of the "first aid" classes, nursing classes of ladies will be held. . _

div.head: RUNCORN WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: RUNCORN WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

A meeting was held in the Union Hall, Runcorn, on Thursday afternoon, in connection with the Central Women's Liberal Federation, and was attended by about fifty ladies. Mr. W. Handley, secretary of the North- wich Division Liberal Association, occupied the chair. After detailing the circumstances which had led to the calling of the meeting, he introduced as representatives from the Central Federation, the Misses Helen B. Tt.om- son and McLaren, Ramsay. These ladies explained in lucid and forcible addresses the objects and work of a branch association, and at the close it was unanimously resolved to at once Dim an asseciation of the ladies pre- sent. A provisional Committee was appointed, with Mrs. Bridgewater as secretary. It.was announced that a further meeting would be held in about a week to re- ceive the provisional Committee's report, and to make permanent arrangements for the success of the associa- tion. Votes of thanks to the ladies for their addresses and the Chairman for presiding brought an interesting meeting to a close.

div.head: THINGS HEARD- AND SEEN AT
div.p: THINGS HEARD- AND SEEN AT
RUNCORN
BY .A.N OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

I was glad to see that the members of the Run- corn Co-operative Society discussed the propriety of helping forward the cause of technical education in Runcorn, at their last meeting. As one of the speakers remarked, it would be a credit to the society if they supported the movement, and a proposal was made to contribute the sum of .£lOO towards the funds for the erection of Runcorn Technical Institute. It was quite fairly contended by Mr. Cosier, that if anything was done in this manner, Widnes ought to be treated in exactly the same way as Runcorn, because half the business of the Society lay in the former town. Eventually, a decision on the subject was deferred until the next half yearly meeting in August next. In describing the Society as a " money grabbing one," Mr. Cosier, ,it must be admitted, vas not far wide of the mark, and it has not done as much as might have been expected for "The social, domestic, and intellectual advancement of its members," which are amongst the objects tor which the Society was established. The fact that thousands of pounds are distributed every six months in the shape of " din i "is emblaz- oned on the hoardings of both Widnes and Runcorn at the present time, and a modest £lOO to the tech- nical school in each town" never would be missed."

The members of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority did good service to the scheme for the construction of a vehicular bridge across the Mersey at the last meeting of Cheshire County Council. Their resolution urging the necessity for such a bridge did good service in giving Mr. Speakman an opportunity of showing that the local authorities of Widnes and Runcorn were in earnest on the subject and that they had got together a mass of informa- tion in regard to the project to lay before the Councils of the two counties whenever a contereace . can be arranged. It is to be hoped ttat tile confer- ence will be held at an early date, in order that ' should the scheme meet with approval, Parliament- ary powers may be obtained next year. Unfortun- ately nothing whatever can be done in that direction this year. It may not be generally known that Mr. Brunner, M.P., during his visit to Runcorn some days ago, inspected the plan of Sir. DJuglas Fox, and made a number of enquiries into the scheme; and being convinced of the great need of vehicular communication between the Runcorn and Widnes districts, will use every means in his power for "obtaining the boon so much desired by the i inhabitants on both sides of the Mersey.

- - It is a sad reflection upon our boasted civilization that the loss of alife is too frequently needed before what are really most serious and obvious defects in railway management of many of our great manu- factories, are remedied. The sacrifice of a young girl on the ship canal railway at Weston Point last week caused a coroner's jury to recommend the. Ship Canal Co. to place gates at the various cross- ings in the neighbourhood, and the representative of the company present promised that this should be done if the Highway Board would consent. I have good reason for stating that the company shortly after their line was constructed undertook, by agreement with the Aaresbury Highway Board, to proteCt the roads, w.hich their line of metals crossed, by properly constructed gates. In the absence of such proteilLion the wonder is that a fatal accident has not occurred before ; of course, the gates will now, no doubt, be provided, but that will be small satisfaction to the bereaved parents of the little one sacrificed on the thar of Laxity.

The balance sheet of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners for the year ended March 25th, 1892, has just been published, and a comparison of a few of the items with those of the previous year may be useful. The total receipts other than from loans ' amounted to £7,505 Is. Id. as against £5,959 10s. 81 in the previous year. The general district rate pro- vided £5,245 Sc. 7d. of that sum, which was con- siderably more than in the preceding year, when the same rate produced only .E 4.779 Is. id. The market rents and tolls produced £50.1 31., against .I;440 15s. 71. ; and niglltsoil sales realised £lB7 Ios. 98., against £ll7 38.61: a considerable im- provement. The total expenditure other than out of loans was £7,286 18s. 51., against £5,558 Ile. 7d.; in the previous year. The chief items are street improvements £3O, against £175 1.0. 21. ; highway repairs £6Bl os. 48., against £132 is. 9]. ; markets £258 181. 103., against £251 15s. 108. ; hospital £7B 14s. 3d., against £l3l Bs. 2d. ; street cleansing £4ll 16s. 9d., against £4lB Os. ; nightsoil removal £l,lOO 14s. 43., against £823 198. Gd. ; salaries, £BlO, against £786 15s. 80. The sum of £953 19s. sd. had! been spent in private improvement work. The ex- ! penditure out of loans was as follow:: t----:ewerage works, £ll4 us. 73 ; Waterloo bridge improvement, £548 178. 83.; Victoria-road, £1,107; total £1,831 16s. 118. In the previous year the expenditure un- der the same head, was sewerage works, .f.:520 ss. 23. ; Waterloo Bridge Improvement, £1,580 14.5. 98. ; nightsoil plant, £245 3s. 88. ; total £2,310 3s. 93. The rateable value of the township cc- cording to the poor rate is £57,153, an increase of nearly £1,700 on the previous yeas ; while the as- sessable value according to the district rate is ! £47,963, an increase also of about £17,000. The ' amount of principal owing on loans was £12,504, as compared with £11,882, in the previous year.

Nothing of an exceptional character trans- pired at the meeting of Widnes Town Council on Tuesday. The Council appropriately acknow- ledged the muniticient gifts to education by Mr. Timmis and the Mayor. The latter gentleman was evidently taken by surprise when the subject was mentioned. and some time elapsed before he replied Ito the vote. The discussion on Alderman Timmis's motion to inquire into the accommodation of the Town Hall, showed that there will be considerable opposition to the completion of that building at the present time. There is no doubt that the present premises are very inadequate for the purposes of the Corporation, and the extension and completion had better be sooner than later so that the towns- people of the present generation may derive some benefit. It is generally expected that the statistics with regard to burial space in the borough asked for by Councillor Hodgkinson, will disclose a con- dition of affairs that will render the provision of a cemetery obligatory in the immediate future.

The Runcorn members of Northwich Division Liberal Association have this week held a meeting and have determined to form a local branch of that Association for the purpose of disseminating poli- tical information, and also for taking part in local elections as well as in Parliamentary contests. There is a strong feeling that local affairs would be better administered were a well organised body to take a part in the elections of members to the several administrative bodies in the town, and also to meet at intervals to discuss questions of interest as they arise. _

div.head: ASSAULT ON A FOREMAN AT WIDNES.
div.p: ASSAULT ON A FOREMAN AT WIDNES.

On Thu7Sl's.: at Widnes Petty Sessions before Mr. A. Walmslev Cothain, and the Mayor, John Lynch a young man, of 29, Beaumont-street, was charged with assault- ing Edward Tanner. Both men were employed at the Widnes Silver and Copper Company's Works. The defen- dant is a furnace man, and the complainant a foreman. On Saturday night the foreman found the defendant asleep, and because he moved him, the defendant threateoed to knock his face off. On Monday night when the. foreman was passing the furnace the defend- ant struck him a blow on the face, giving him a black I eye. A scuffle ensued, and Mr. Wilkins, the manager of the copper department, separated the men, and dis- charged the defendant from the works.—The defendant alleged that he did not assault the complainant ; it was a fight, and he called a witness in his behalf.—Mr. W. T. Husband, who prosecuted for the company, said the directors did not press for a heavy penalty.—The Bench imposed a fine of 2s. ed. and costs 10s. 61.

div.head: WIFE'S TROUBLES AT WIDNES.
div.p: A WIFE'S TROUBLES AT WIDNES.

William Hallam, of Manchester, was brought before the Widnes Bench of Magistrates on Thursday to show cause why he should not maintain his wife zillati Hallam. —Mr. .1. W. Knowles represented the complainant, who stated that she had been married to the defendant eleven years. Three years ago he broke up the furniture of their home at Widnes and then left her destitute. From that time until six weeks ago, she was supported by her son. At the beginning of the year the defendant wrote asking her to go to his brother's house at Manchester, and she went, but after staying there three weeks, she came to the conclusion that he was too intimate with his brother's wife, and then defendant took a room in another part of Manchester. They stayed thcre a couple of weeks, and then defendant deserted her again. She was destitute, and was without food until Wednesday when she walked to her son's house at Widnes.—The magistrates made an order upon the defendant to con- tribute 53. per week towards his wife's maintenance.

Birkett Musgrove was the accompanist. A WIDNES BARBER AND Ills BEFACTORY APPRENTICE. At Widnes County Court yesterday before his Honour, Judge Shand, Joseph Barton, 15 years of age, residing at 29, Widnes-road, sued VVilliain Jones, hairdresser, fa, Widnes-road, for £5O damages for breach of an agree- ment.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys (Runcorn) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. G. Steele, barrister, Liver- peel instructed by Mr. F. ,T. Poole, defended. It anpeared that on the Ist January, 1891, after the plaintiff had been in the defendant's employ for some months lie and his father signed indentures with the defendant tor five years, the weekly wage to rise from 6s. to 12s. On the 22nd October lase, at night the defendant complained of the unsatisfactory manner with which he had lathered a customer, and told him he deserved punching out of the soup. The youth replied that he could walk out without being punched. At half past eleven the de- fendant called the plaintiff into the kitchen, gave him his wages, and asked him wiles lie meant by his insol- ence. The youth said he was not going to be made a fool of before a shop full of customers, whereupon the defendant tore the indentures into scraps and threw the pieces behind the fire and told the lad he was free to go where he liked. The defence was that the plaintiff had performed his work very unsatisfactorily and that the indentures were can- celled by mutual agreement. Mr. Steele argued that asthe father had signed the indentures the plaint if could not possibly sue.—Mr. Humphreys quoted decisions to show that an infant could not possibly rescind his in- dentures, unless it was conclusively proved that it was for his material benefit to, do so. This had not been done.—The Judge held that the plaintiff, cou'cl sue and gave a verdict tor £2 with costs.

On Friday evening last week,the teachers and friends of this institution held a social evening. The large in- fants' school was converted in the one one 'part into a drawing-room, and the second part into a dining-room, the wank being undertaken by the ladies, Mrs. Tonks having full charge of the arrangements. ACCIDENTS ON THE SHIP CANAL. WORES AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday morning, William Brown, aged 13, residing at 60, Halton-road, sustained rather severe injuries whilst engaged in swinging a large piece of rock suspended from the chain of a crane. He miscal- culated the necessary force to be applied for swinging the stono to a required spot, and it struck him in the region of the abdomen with considerable force. He was rendered unconscious, and the unfortunate lad is suffer- ing from internal injuries.--at eight o'clock the same morning a labourer named Thompson, aged 40, of Run- corn, was seriously injured at the la.ttom of the Bridge- water lock. Whilst in a stooping posture a piece of plank fell a distance of about 30 feet on to his back. He was picked up unconscious, and immediately trans- ferred to Latchford Hospital. Before Sir Richard Brooke and Mr. Henry lleynolds,at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, James Millington, a disreputable looking man, was charged with having on the 6th February threatened his wife Jane.—The coin- plaMant said the defendant left her seven years ago with seven children and he had never lived with her since. On Monday last he came to her house and struck the knife produced kapparently a sailor's sheath knife) into the door, an said she had not many hours to live. On the Saturday previous he had told her that she might count her hours; the children had been without a father and they would he without a mother soon.—Superinten- dent Atherton said the prisoner had been convicted of all kinds of offences.—Tho Bench ordered him to be bound

over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO and one surety in £5, or in default a month's hard labour. The prisoner said he would go to god and left the dock saying "Good morning Jane."
