PROPOSED PURCHASE OF RUNCORN WATERWORKS. -
LIVELY MEETING OF RATEPAYERS. On Thursday night a public meeting of ratepayers was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, to consider _ . _ _ _ _ .

. _ certain resolutions passed by the Board of Commis- sioners ou November 28th, and if thought desirable to pass a resolution confirming them and auth- orising the Commissioners to promote a Bill in Parliament to acquire the undertaking of the Runcorn, Weston and Halton Waterworks Co. There was a large attendance. Mr. F. Wiswall presided, and on the platform were Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., J. Pritchard, J. Meadowcroft, E. Wynne Humphreys. W. Fisher, J. W. Lightburn, B. Bisbrown, F. A. Lake (law clerk) and E. Marshall (secretary). The Chairman submitted the following resolution: "That this meeting, as representing the owners and ratepayers of the district ot the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, do, pursuant to the provisions of the Act of the 35th and 36th Victoria, chapter 91, intituled • An act to authorize the application of funds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies in certain cases,' approve of, and consent ta the following resolu- tions of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, passed at their meeting held in the Town Hall, Runcorn, on the 28th ef November, 1892, namely: 'That applica- tion be made to Pirliament in the session of 1893, for a

--- bill to provide for the purchase by the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, compulsorily or by agree- ment, of the undertaking of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company, the winding up and dis- solution of the company, the extension of powers for the local government of the district, the amendment of Acts, and for other puposes. That the cost charges, and expenses preliminary and incidental to the applying for, promotion, and passing such Bill into an Act shall be charged upon the general district rate.'"

The Chairman, proceeding, said that there were many things in common that they as a community could not do without, and in their case it was water. The pre- sent occasion seemed to be a favourable opportunity for obtaining the control of the water supply. The Water Company wero not able to meet the whole of the re- quirements of the town, and were disposed to sell their undertaking. The Commissioners were unanimous in the opinion that they ought to come to terms, and they felt every confidence in asking the ratepayers to support them in their negstiations. They 'ere not asked to

commit themselves to the purchase of the undertaking, for the Commissioners assured them that they did not intend to "pay through the nose." They were deter- mined to protect their interests in every direction. Every scrutiny had been made in the consideration of the matter. The Commissioners were not in a position to give them a specific statement as to the course of the negotiations, as they were still pending. They were only asking for powers to purchase the works if they could come to terms without trespassing on their pockets. The rates should not be burdened by the transaction. If the Commissioners got the powers they asked for, whether they bought the undertaking or not, they would be able to prevent the Waterworks Company indulging in a "dog in the manger" policy. , They wished to be placed in that position that the trade I of the place should not be plaaed in jeopardy for want of water. Trades and manufacturers were wanting water and could not get it, and they must have some • means of getting a supply. , Mr. Pritchard kchairman of the Parliamentary Corn- : mittße), in seconding the adoption of the resolution, said that the Commissioners deemed the present occa- sion a favourable one for the acquisition of the water- 1-works. With a view of accomplishing that object, the I Commissioners had been supplied with balance sheets from the Water Company: It was understood that the one for the year ending June 30th should be accepted as the basis upon which some arrangement should be made. That statement showed a profit of £l,BOO available for ordinary dividend. After investigation, the Commissioners arrived at the conclusion that a fair price to offer would be on an average a profit of £1,575, being the profit available for the ordinary capital, and upon that profit they concluded to pay 25 years' pur- chase. On the preference shares they proposed to pay 28 years' purchase. These terms he considered most favourable, compared with the amounts usually ob- tained in regard to saunter works. The provisional agreement made was baseJ on those terms ; they would give a capital amount of £67,500. If they rejected the resolution it would be equivalent to saying they would not have the works at any price. Mr. Walter Collier inquired if it was not the case that the Water Company were, by their Act of Parliament, bound to give an adequate supply of water. The Chairman replied that they were for domestic purposes. Mr. Collier asked if in the event of the ratepayers refusing to senctioa the expenditure entailed in the pro- motion of the Bill requiring powers for the acquisition of the Waterworks, the Commissioners would be surcharged with the expenditure. (Loud applause.) Eie also desired to be Informed whether the Commis- sharers ought not to have corns* to the ratepayers before the Bill was deposited in Parliament. - (Applause.) Mr. Lake replied that the meeting had been called in a legal manner. It was not usual to come to the rate- payers until the Bill was deposited, and two meetings of the Commissioners had been held. With regard to the surcharge the Commissioners were technically liable, hut by appealing to the Local Government Board con- sent could he obtained to charge it on the rates, and the amount would be laid on the rates current for the year, whereas under the ordinary conditions it could be spread over ten years. The costs would raise the rates by 21d. in the £. In reply to other remarks, the Law Clerk said the Company had no water to supply for trade pur- poses. there had • been cases of people who wanted water for trade purposes being refused —bricirmalting and things of that kiwi. Mr. Collier : And breadbaking. (Laughter.)—The water had been cut off repeatedly. Mr. Collier further said the ratepayers ought to be informed of the nature of the hitch in the accounts, as discovered by the audi- tor. Everythingssuaht to be placed "square and above- board." (Loud applause.) Mr. Langshaw asked if the Commissioners had not a report from the analyst that the water was not pure. The Chairman said the water compared favourably with the water supplies of other authorities, where they got water from the red sandstone, which was noted for hardnesss but also for remarkable freedom from organic matter. Mr. I. Bowyer asked if they were to understand that the water was worse now than it was when the company got their Bill. If so, it must have materially deterior- ated the value of the works. Tire Chairmah said Mr. Bowyer was quite correct,and they were watching the matter very carefully. It was because the well was drawn upon to that extent that the saltnnd lime were drawn upon excessively, and below the sea level. If the water was drawn from a higher level, as it used to be, they would get a better supply. Mr: Bowyer was in favour of the town having the water supply, but he was not willing to purchase it at an exorbitant price. If the water was going worse and diminishing, the works would soon be not worth a £5 note. The Chairman explained that the water in the well was not diminishing in quantity, but it would not meet the requirements of the town Mr. Bowyer stated the difficulty he had experienced in obtaining water at his house. Mr. Langshaw said that they had been practically without water for ten days. Other ratepayers made similar complaints, awl the Chairman said that was an arrangement in favour of the Commissioners. Mr. Coventry considered the present company would have to make a considerable =lay to provide a suffici- ent supply. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys stated that whatever might be said by sneering critics, the only gentlemen who were capable of forming a judgment upon this matter were the members who sat round the Board of Com- missioners. This created a great uproar. There was stamping of feet, and loud cries of " question " and " withdraw," i and one ratepayer exclaimed "he shan't speak if we stay here all Ili& unless he withdraws." Eventually upon Mr. Humphreys resuming his seat, Mr. Kniveton said they asked for the withdrawal of the words sneering . . crams. (Applause.)—Mr. Bowyer : Am Lone he alludes Ito P—Mr. Humphreys : Emphatically no. He did not I apply the word sneering to any gentleman who had I spoken. It 'Would have been more courteous to have allowed him to finish the sentence. Continuing he said the reason—not that he claimed for himself or any mem- ber of the Board superior judgment—that he made the statement was simply because the gentlemen around the Board were the only persons so far, who had all the in- formation at their disposal, which could enable them • to arrive at a correct conclusion.—Mr. W. Handley said e when the ratepayers were asked to spend something h £67,500, they ought to know the basis on which the _om e - missioners were acting. What was the net revenue of the Company P—Mr. Lake replied that after paying _interest on debenture stock there was an amount of £l,BOO avail- able for dividend on ordinary shsres.—Mr. Haniley : But a mistake bas been found in the figures of the Company. How much was the annual income reduced ? —Mr. Lake said that was a matter they could not agree upon. The Commissioners' accountant said the income was £6OO less thanrepresented.— Mr.flandlev said assumisg the accountant's figures were correct there was an income, and taking the purchase price at£67,000 which the Company were determined to have, there would be a charge of aso per annum upon the rates, which meant that the district rate would be increased by 4ad. in the L. Could they afford that in addition to the present rate of 2s. 4d. ? (Loud cries of "No.') The Chairman : We have told the meeting We do not intend to give £67,000 for the undertaking. • Mr. Handley said the ratepayers before they voted any sum of money ought to know what the Commis- sioners intended to give. Mr. R. Posnett centended that the waterawas unsuit- able for manufacturing purposes and ruined boilers. The Chairman said he was quite aware of the fact, and the Commissioners wisned to tap theVyrewy supply, which was eminently suitable for boilers and could be placed at the disposal of manufacturers.

Mr. Lightlaurn pointed out that they could not get that supply without purchasing the waterworks. Mr. Meadowcroft agreed that the Waterworks would become a paying concern in a very short period of time.

Mr. P. Speakman, whom the Chairman introduced as the largest property owner in the town, supported the resolution, and said as a ratepayer he was willing to tax • his pocket a little at the commencement, because he be- lieved that in the immediate future the ratepayers would receive great benefit if the Commissioners ac- quired the waterworks. He knew an industry that was languishing, and men had not been doing anything for twelve months, because the Company could not give them water to make bricks with. They were soon to have the Ship Canal open, and there would be many works built in tileir midst, if thy could only be in a position to supply them with water, and the ratepayers would make a very great mistake if they refused to pass the resolution.

Mr. Handley suggested that when the Commissioners had provisionally agreed upon the price with the Water- works Co., tho matter should be submitted to a future meeting of the ratepayers, and the Chairman having given an undertaking to this effect, which it was under- stood would be recorded, the resolution was carried, only three hands being held up against. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting, which had occupied over two hours.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
ThE PURCHASE OF THE WATERWORKS.

A special meeting of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners was held on Tuesday night for the pur- pose of receiving and considering a recommendation of the Finance and Parliamentary Committee se- Runcorn Water Bill. Mr. F. Wiswall presided and there were present Messrs. Fisher, Humphreys, Bisbrown, Lea, Lightburn, Speakman, Pritchard, Lake (law clerk), and Marshall secretary. The Finance and Parliamentary Committee presented the following report as to the terms of purchase and al- teration in Bill :—" Your Committee have received the report of Mr. Tunstall, on the books and accounts and the report of Mr. Newton, on the work and plant of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company, duly considered the seise, and found them unsatisfac- tory. By the instructions the Law Clerk wrote to the solicitor to the Waterworks Company on the sth Jan. last, asking that an allowance should be made in res- pect of defective works, and that the purchase money should be reduced in proportion to the reduction in profits shown by Mr. Tunstall. No definite reply to that letter was received but on the second inst. a statement was submitted by Mr. Ashton, purporting to show what the profits of the Company might be if the aecounts were collected in a different manner to that adopted in the past. On the 3rd inst. your Committee considered this statement in conjunction with the previous correspondence, and in- structed the Law Clerk to write requesting a definite reply to the points raised in his letter of the sth ult., not later than the 9th inst., and also to arrange for Mr. Tunstall to consider Mr. Ashton's statement, and attend here on Monday next for that purpose. The Law Clerk wrote as instructed, namely :—" Runcorn, 4th February 1893. Dear Sir,—Re-Waterwcrks. At a meeting of nay clients held last evening, the correspondence between us, commencing with my letter of the sth ultimo and ending with your statement as to what the income of your clients company might be under certain possible circumstance was considered. As ample time for the checking of your accounts as stated in your letter of 17th ultimo, has elapsed, and you do not appear to dis- pute the correctness of Mr. Tunstall's figures,but instead open up an entirely new and hypothetical basis for cal- culation. lam instructed to ask you for a categorical reply to the points raised in my letter of the sth ultimo, not later than the afernoon of Wednesday. I may say that the advertisement for the public meeting will appear nest week, so that we must be in a position to decide on what lines we shall proceed at our adjourned meeting on Thursday morning.—Yours truly, FRED A. LAXII. J. Ashton, Esq., solicitor." He had received the following reply. " Magistrates' Clerk Office, Runcorn Bth February, 1893. Dear sir,— Waterworks.—ln reply to your letter of the sth of January last, I am instructed to say with reference to the defects mentioned by Mr. Newton, my clients would point out that by clause 6 of the agreement they are to "continue to keep the works in good and proper order, " repair and condition, (reasonable wear and tear and " accidents and strikes of workmen excepted)," but if you think this is not sufficient to warrant your calling upon them to provide a new boiler, I may state that they .consider a new boiler is required, and it is their intention to provide one during the coming summer, and I may also add that they have had an estimate made by a competent engineer of the cost of the repairs neces- sary to the engine, which amounts to about £BO, and these repairs they are also prepared to do. With reference to the amount of the purchase money I am instructed to say that independently of the question as to whether Mr. Tunstall is right or wrong in his calculations, or whether the estimated income is more or less than £1,575, the Directors are not prepared to advise the Company to accept a less susn than £67,soo.—Yours truly, Josni Ammon. F. A. Liam, ESQ. Mr.Tunstall attended at the Law Clerks' Office on Mon- day evening and met Mewrs. Fisher and Hankinsen in consultation, when he was requested to consider the prospective income of the waterworks undertaking, and report on the proposed purchase independently ot any proposed extension of works by Thursday next. After considering Mr. Tunstalls report, your Committce recommend (1) That a letter be sent to the Waterworks Company acknowledging their promise to make good their defects specified by Mr. Newton, and pointing out the &presentations and basis on which and reciting how the proposed purchase modey of £67,500 was arrived at and stating that independently of the legal aspect of the agreement the Company are bound in honour to reduce the purchase money in so far as such representations and basis have been proved to be mistaken. (2) That in case the Company refuse to reduce the said purchase money to such a sum as may be agreed upon between them and the Commissioners, clause 6 in the Runcorn ; Water Bill now before Parliament, be withdrawn and a , clause giving power to purchase the waterworks under- taking either by agreement or arbitration be substituted , therefore, and the other consequent alterations made in ' the Bill."
The report was adopted on the moticn of Mr. Pritchard seconded by Mr. Speakman, after a lengthy deliberation in private.

div.head: WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB.

Tha annual meeting of the Warrington Cycling Club was held at the Norton Arms Hotel on Thurs- day evening. Mr. D. Tinnion occupied the chair. The report of Mr. E. Pickavance, secretary, stated that the attendance prizes had been won by Ist W. Mountield, 2nd E. Pickavance., jun., and 3rd J. Podmore. A 100 miles road competition has been held resulting as follows: Gold medals, E. Pickavance, jun., and J. Waddington. Gold centre medals. F. Wilson, F. Molvneux, 11. Hope. and F. Barber. Silver medal, S. CaCik. An athletic meeting has been held which was eminently successful, the club championship falling to the lot of W. H. Bellian for the 2nd time in succession, the 2nd place being held by uckt on , and the 3rd by T. Hope. During the season two fancy dress and lantern parades have been organized, the first,which was truly a gorgeous spectacle, being in aid of the funds of the Warrington Ragged School. The wait of the collection was £lB. The second :was quite as good a display as the first, and the collection, which was in aid of the iVarrington Gymnasium, resulted in the matter of £Blos. being raised.. A billiard handicap, which has caused much competition, has resulted in the following receiving prizes : Messrs. J. Buxton, Calvert, J. Pod- more, and D. Tinnion. The. Treasurer's balance sheet shows a healthy state of affairs ; after paying all expgnses the club will have a balance of £5 to start with next season. Therefore, taking all things into consideration, the Club is in a prosperous condition, and by the end of next season should rank first among the Cycling Clubs of North of England. The following officers were elected : —Mr. T. Morris, president, and Mr. W. Pierpoint, Tice- president. Mr. E. Pickavance, sec. ; Mr. J. Crltchley. trea. ; a committee consisting of Messrs. Wm. Browne,, W. Bellian, J. E. Warren, R. Fair, J. Podmore, T. Davies, and S. Wright, J.P., was appointed. Messrs. T. Pemberton and T. Cooper were appointed auditors.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
AMBULANCE CLAM.

A class has been started at Penketh for the in-- struction of first aid to the wounded. The promo- ter is the Rev. J. R. Jones, and the teacher is Dr. A. Murray. The class is in connection with the Pen- keth Church Mission Sunday School, and will be under the auspices of the St. John's Ambulance Society. On Thursday night the class met for the first time, and the Rev. J. It. Jones explained the uses of the class, and then Dr. Murray gave the lecture, which was very interesting and was illus- trated with diagrams. There was a good attend- ance. •

MUTUAL IMPROVEMINT OD Wednesday last the usual meeting of the above was held in the Wesleyan School. Mr. James. Watson was in the chair. Mr. John Peers gace a paper on " Vivisection " which proved very in- interesting. After the paper several of the mon- hers asked questions, and discussed the paper. PLOUGHING. On Thursday the farmers from Penketh and its outskirts turned out :-;) give a day's work to Mr 4, Harrison, the new tenant at Cderdley Hall. ?Cis an old custom for the farmers to give a day's Ivo& to a newcomer, and on Thursday the farmers of Penketh and neighbourhood were well represented. The various teams were from Penketh, Sankey, Cuerdley, Buttonwood.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
CORRECTION.

Last week it was st;-t—ed--1;--the'se columns that three persons, charged with discharging fireworks in Enuts- ford-road, were teachers at the Emmanuel Church Sunday School. It shoold have been stated that they were simply connected with that Sunday School.

- APPLICATION FOR A DANCING LmEsisn. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before Alderman Holmes (chairman), Alderman Chand- ley, and Mr. F. W. Monks, Mr. P. Davies applied on be- half of Thomas Hill, wire drawer and dancing master, Marsh House Farm, for a dancing license for a dancing class in an upper storey of Jones's boiler works. Mr. Davies said the applicant had been 21 years in the em- ploy of Messrs. Rylands Bros., and was a most respect- able man, and of good character. The class was for- merly conducted by Mr. Hill and Mr. Broadhurst, and Mr. Hill, taking his word that he could do all the legal work,had allowed hien previously to apply for a licence, but was astonished to find when he appeared in court, that instead of his being well up in law and well in with the magistrates, the reverse was the case. This class was going to be carried on in a proper manner, and Mr. Hill, being wishful to have the protection of the police for the sake of law and order.applied for the license. The class would meet from 7.30 p.m. to 10 p.m. on Monday, Wed- nesday, and Friday.evenings, but the applicant wished fer the time to be up till 10.30, to allow time for the room being cleared. There would be admission only to members, except the police, who would be the only free members, and they could see the list of names of mem- bers at any time.—The Chairman (Alderman Holmes)!: How about refreshments ?—Mr. Davies : Oh, there are no refreshments.—Mr. Davies said the applicant was a man of most respectable character, and Canon Dodd would have been present to speak as to his character, he having conducted dancing at Stretten, but was from home. Mr. Davies read a letter from Mr. James Howard, parish clerk at Stretton, who, he said, acted as M.C. for annual dances at Stretton, which testified to Mr. Hill's good character, and Canon Dodd's good opinion of him. Mr. Davies also mentioned that Mr. Hill had conducted a dancing class at Marsh House Farm.—The Chief Con-
A

stable gave the applicant an excellent character, but raised some objection to there being no place of egress apart from the entrance, and to the room teing lit with parraffin lamps. He mentioned that there were 50 license houses which had a license for singing and music, including 9 beerhouses, and only one licensed house which had a license for dancing, but there were ten other places, such as the Workmen's Club, for in- stance, which had licenses for dancing.—Mr. F. Monks said there were two sorts of dancing classes, one where the dancing was of the go-as-you-please description, ar.d there was no instruction, and the other where the steps were taught.—Mr. Hill informed the Bench that his class would be of the latter sort, and not a mere con- tinuation of the class previously held in the building.— The license was granted subject to Mr. Hill making cer- tain alterations for the convenience of the public, to the satisfaction of Mr. Hunt. The Chairman: I am frightened of the paraffin, though : you should have gas. —Mr. Davies : We will see. It is rather poor gas. (Laughter.) A LIVERPOOL-ROAD RESIDENT IN TROUBLE. On Saturday morning, Sophia Eggington, a married woman, living in Liverpool-rood,was charged with hav- ing made use of threats towards Esther Ashcroft, a nsighbour.—Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the com- plainant, stated the facts of the case.—Esthdr Ashcroft, living at 113, Liverpool-road, bore out Mr. Browne's statements' and said she was afraid of the defendant on account of the threats which she had used towards her. She never felt safe, even when in her own house. , Detective Monaghan stated that he apprehended the 1 defendant on Friday. He went dowq to her house, and I was admitted by the little boy. The defendant was sit- ting in the kitchen when he went in. She had neither shoes nor stocking on one of her feet. He told her what he had come for, and she instantly jumped up, and picking up the poket told him she would give him the "soft end of it on the head." He called in two other constables, and they tried to persuade her to put on her shoe and stocking. She refused, and they proceeded to take her to the Police Station. When she got outside she said she would put them on if they would let her go back. They did so, but on reaching the kitchen again she sat down and said she was not going to put them on. They then took her out again towards the station. When Sankey-street was reached the defendant got a cab and they drove the rest of the way. The Chairman (Mr. Burgess) said that he was sorry to see the defend- ant in the dock, but the case had been clearly proved, and there was no alternative. She would have to find a surety of £lO to keep the peace for six months, or go to gaol for two months without hard labour. The de- fendant was led out of court crying bitterly.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes (chairman) and Messrs. F. Monks, W. Pierpoint. J. W. Hayward, and S. Wright, Major Pickmere, and Captain

Ridgway. WIFE ASSMILT.-Wm. McAuley, iron moulder, 166, Winwick-street, was charged with assaulting his wife Elizabeth, on the previous Friday. The complainant said he struck and kicked her in the morning and then west out and got some drink, and came in, and in the evening attacked her agai n.—A female witness who lived with the parties corroborated, and said James Sheridan (a lodger) and the defendant were struggling together and the complainant was trying to separate them.— James Sheridan said the defendant quarrelled with his wife and called witness "her fancy lodger," and assaulted him, he striking in self defence.—The defend- ant : Marks were all over my body.—Witness : And me too.—lnspector Spinks said the defendant had formerly been in the Rainhill Asylum, and endeavours had been made to get him there again, but as the doctor would not sign the certificate, a warrant was taken out. He was jealous of his wife, and said she wanted him at Rainhill so that she could live with the lodger.—The defendant said he had got Sheridan work and kept him, and since he came out of the asylum Sheridan had not behaved as a man to him.—Mr. Watmough deposed that he had known the defendant 21 years, and never knew anything against him.—A medical certificate of his recovery was put in, and the defendant was bound over to keep the peace for 3 months and had to pay ss. costs. •

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Smith, labourer. in Buttermarket-street, on Sunday afternoon, ss. or 7 days' imprisonment. —Peter Rourke in Corporation-street, on Saturday afternoon, dismissed.—Henry Geary, a lab- ourer, in Golden Square, on Saturday night, the defend- ant stating that he took a few glasses on account of the smallpox being about, and they took effect on him, dis- missed with a caution.—John Lavrenson, 37, Chorler street, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Rylands-street, on Saturday night, and with assaulting George Lemon, a man of colour, on the same occasion. —A constable, the complainant Lemon, and another witness proved the case. Lemon said the defendant asked him far a penny and because he did not give him one used bad language to him. Witness told him he

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 18, 1893.

ought to be ashamed of himself, and then the defendant struck hitn.—The defendant was fined ss. and costs, 12s. 6d. in all.—Edward Lucy was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mersey-street on Saturday night. He commenced his misconduct in tke street, and P.C. Amson got him into his house, then he came to the bedroom window and cursed and swore there.—He was dismissed with a caution. DM:Ml.—Thomas Mitchell, in Rose and Crown-street, on Saturday night was dismissed. INDECENT CONDUCT.—Mary O'Reilly WES charged with this behaviour in Market-st., on Saturday night, aud also with having been previously convicted of the offence, and went to jail for a month. THIMSDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (in the chair), Alderman Sutton, and Captain Ridgway. THEFT OF LEAD.—HsAvy PBNALT2.—A man named John Smith, a slater, formerly in the employ of Mr. Jos. Mounfield, was charged with stealing on the 18th Jan., 2cwts. of lead piping, and on the 23rd lcwt. of lead piping, the property of Mr. Joseph Mounfield, and valued at about 193. The Chief Constable in opening the case said that nothing was heard by the police of the theft until the previous day, when they received infor- mation from Mr. Holland, fruiterer, of Crown-st., that during the early part of the morning he went into his yard, which is close to that of Mr. Taylor, marine store dealer. He there found a bag containing a quantity of lead piping. There was no one about, so he took the bag and concealed it and presently saw the prisoner coming looking for it. When prisoner asked him if he had seen the bag, he answered in the affirmative. Prisoner then said it was his and that he wanted it. Mr. Holland said he could have it if he would come down to the Police Station with him. Prisoner con- sented to do this, but ran away down an entry in Win- wick-street. Mr. Holland gave information to the police and D.S. Monozhan visited the shop of Mr. Taylor, marine store dealer, and found on the books entries of the stolen property. Prisoner was then ar- rested in a house in School Brow. The lead found by Mr. Holland was supposed to have been stolen from Stockton Heath.—Further evidence was given by Mr. Joseph Mounfield, and prisoner, who pleaded guilty to the theft was sentenced to three month's imprison- ment. Inspector Norman, who was corroborated by several witnesses, gave evidence show- ing that the houses named were unsanitary in conse- quence of bad spouts, defective cistern piping, damp walls and damp uatiled scullery floors. The defendants had been served with a notice in November, but had not complied with it. BREACHES or THE COAL MINES ACT.—Charles For- thaw, miner, was eharged by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Haydock, with committing a breach of the above-named Act, by neglecting to sprag up the roof where hp was working at Bostock colliery so as to pre- vent a fall of coal. A representative of the firm of Messrs. Peace and Ellis, sacitors, of Wigan, appeared for the prosecution. It appeared that the defendant had left the spot in question, and a few hours after the roof fell in at the identical place. No other workmen had been engaged at that particular place, but though he had not endangered others, he had imperilled his own life.—The defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 10s. and costs.—Alfred Barnes, Haydock, was charged with a breach of the special rule 148 relating to the duties of colliers, on January 19th. The defendant, who pleaded guilty, was in charge of the ventilating apparatus of the Wood Pit, Haydock, where one hundred and fifty lives were lost many years since in an explosion, and on the day in question he was found asleep by the side of one of the furnaces which regulated the ventilation of the mine. One of the furnaces was completely out, and the other was on the verge of expiring. On that particular day it was all the more necessary that defendant should have paid unusual care to his charge, as the only other furnace was under repairs, consequently the whole of the ventilating apparatus was under his charge. There were at the time 119 men in the mine' all of whose lives had been seriously jeopardized. The defendant, after being severely censured, was fined 20s. and costs.

div.head: COTTON OPERATIVES REMAIN FIRM.
div.p: COTTON OPERATIVES REMAIN FIRM.

A meeting of the general body of delegates to the Amalgamated Association of Operative. Cotton Spinners was held on Saturday in Manchester, for the purpose of considering any proposals that might be made with re- gard to the wages dispute in South-east Lancashire. , Mr. Thomas Ashton (Oldham) presided, and every dis- trict in the Amalgamation was represented. It was reported that the opinion of the district associations was unanimously against any acceptance of the reduc- tion of 5 per cent. A resolution was unanimously carried—" That the Executive Committee be instructed under no circumstances to accept the reduction." Re- solutions were also passed affirming that the Executive Council had used every legitimate means to bring the crisis to a close, expressing confidence in the Council, and agreeing that in future half lock-out pay should be distributed—except in the cases of children— in order that the Amalgamation might be enabled" to carry on the struggle indefinitely." The Card and Blowing Room operatives also held a meeting on Satur- day, and reported that their districts were unanimously firm against the acceptance of the proposed reduction.
ACTION OF THE MASTERS.-MORE MILLS TO BE CLOSED.

On Tuesday, a meeting of the committee of the Employers' Federation, was held in Manchester; to con- sider the replies to the circular sent out by the federa- tion asking the owners of mills where work has not been stopped to close their works absolutely from the 25th inst. It was stated by the secretary that owners repre- senting 2,000,000 spindles had agreed to close. These are in ae,dition to the mills already closed. The remain- ing federationalists had agreed conditionally to work short time. The decision will affect about 2,000 operatives, whose contributions to the levy will be stopped ; while, on the other hand, they will now be claimants for relief day. On Friday the situation will be laid before a meeting of the federationalists, whose opinion generally is that, notwithstanding that they have gone on half-pay, the operatives will not be able to hold out for any great length of time.

POLITICAL PROPAGANDISM.
AN EXAMPLE WORTH FOLLOWING.

_ During the past few days several most successfcl meetings have been held in the quarry districts of Carnarvonshire. when Mr. Robert Williams (Carnarvon) gave a series of of his pictorial lectures on political his- tory. Mr. Williams is well-known throughout North and South Wales as a fluent and forcible speaker in Welsh and English, and in order to illustrate his re- marks in the most telling manner,he has lately designed a large number of slides especially prepared to depict the various episodes in political history of the past 15 years, as well as the chief political topics of the period. The pictures are generally authentic, and are inters- persed with some most appropriate sketches and car- toons, the whole being cleverly manipulated with a limelight lantern. At Llandegai, Tregartb, Bethesda. and other places the meetings were densely packed, and though the audiences in each case were mainly composed of Gladstonians, the proceedings everywhere were most orderly, and the lectures thoroughly enjoyed and ap- preciated.

div.head: PURSUED BY HOUNDS. TERRIBLE RACE FOR LIFE.
div.p: PURSUED BY HOUNDS. TERRIBLE RACE FOR LIFE.

On Saturday afternoon last the Hoylake Harriers Club had arranged their usual week-end run, the route chosen being to Moreton and back. The " hares," Willie Cump- sty and Willie Eccles, proceeded to lay the paper trail, and had got about half the distance to Moreton when they heard the baying of hounds afar off. They took no notice of this, and proceeded with their paper distribu- tion, but as the cry of the hounds became louder and every moment louder still they began to get anxious and climbed a hedge to make investigations. They saw the dogs about two fields off coming straight in their direc- tion, and it dawned upon them that the animals had taken up their trail, and if overtaken by them they would be surely torn to pieces. There was no place of refuge in the immediate vicinity, but a farm house lay about half a mile away, towards which the boys set off at full speed. Being capital sprinters they made the pace hot, but, unfortunately, in climbing over a fence, Cumpsty got fast in some barbed wire, and in the few moments it took to get disengaged it lessened the distance between them and their pursuers. The dogs had now sighted them, and with howls and yells set after them. The boys ran for dear life, a very few yards separating them from what would be a cruel death. They were now rapidly approaching the farmyard, and there was still a hope for them. They rushed wildly on, almost blinded ley exhaustion, across the farmyard. The stable door was open, and they sprang in just as the dogs was enter- ing the yard. They banged the door to not a moment too soon, and set their backs against it, for as they did the hounds came bounning up, foiled of their prey, and howling and yelling in mad chorus. It was not long before the huntsmen arrived and whipped the dogs away, and when they had taken their departure the poor youths emerged from their haven of refuge half dead with fright and exhaustion, and returned home, the paper chase of the Hoylake Harriers Club spoiled for that day. It appears that the dogs were the Wirral Beagles, for which an aniseed trail had been laid, which the boys must have crossed, taking the scent up on their feet and thus diverting the dogs on to their track, with the result described.

PRESENTATION TO A RAILWAY OFFICIAL AT RCSCORN.

Mr. It; Smith, who for the past eight years has been stationmaster at Runcorn, was the recipient Of a handsome and valuable silver-plated tea and : coffee service, suitably inscribed, from toe staff of the station on Monday evening. .Mr. Smith had lately been removed to Lowton, near Newton-le- Willows, to take charge.of the station there, and the local servants of the Company felt that they could not allow him to depart without some token of the res- pect in which they held him, and of the appreciation in L which they held his character. Commencing as a " Num- ber taker" at Edge Hill, 42 years ago, Mr. Smith has a life-long experience of railway work. His father was a railway servant for 30 years and met with his death whilst in the discharge 'of his duties. Mr. Smith had passed through the various grades to the rank of station- master, in which latter capacity he had officiated at Lancaster and Bolton; previous to being placed in charge of Runcorn station. His reminiscenses of railway life would form an interesting volume,and he had not passed through his long servitude without some of those excit- ing and dangerous adventures which befall many of the men who work upon the line. At the station of which he now has the control, Mr. Smith was once run over whilst acting as guard, and at the same time his coat was blown to tatters by four exploding fog signals. Three months in the Liverpool Infirmary followed this accident. Mr. Smith was also severely injured on another occasion. Early in his career, Mr. Smith was sent to London in charge of a mortar, which was des- tined to take part ,in ,the seige of Sebastopol during the Crimean War, and he was present at the banquet given at the opening of Crewe Works, nearly half a century ago. During his stay in Runeorn,he has by his unfailing courtesy and attention won the esteem and good will of the travelling public, and his departure was the cause of considerable regret. The ceremony on Monday evening, took place in the Gentlemen's Waiting Room, in the pre- sence of a large number of railway men. Mr. Rhodes, the new Stationmaster, was also present.—Mr. Newton (chief clerk), said he was pleased to be present on that occasion for the purpose of presenting their late station- master, Mr. Smith, with a beautiful tea and coffee ser- vice, as a token of esteem from the staff of the station. He was sure he spoke the sentiments of all present and, of every subscriber, when he expressed regret at Mr. ' Smith's removal from amongst them. Mr. Smith and himself had worked together for nearly eight years at , Runcorn under very exceptional circumstances. He doubted not many present would be surprised to learn that the traffic receipts at Runcorn Station had simply doubled during that time as Mr. Smith and he knew to their cost because,unfortunately the staff had not grown with the increase of traffic. Anyone who had any ac- quaintance with railway work would know what that , meant to heads of departments ;it meant extra labour , both mental and physical. Mr. Smith had always been , equal to any emergency, and he had ever been alive to the interests of the Company, while at the same time, he had done his best to help the staff under his charge. The I staff and subscribers hoped that Mr. Smith would accept that present not so much for its intrinsic value as for the good wishes that accompanied it. (Applause.)—Mr. Smith said he was taken quite by surprise. When Mr. Newton told him that a deputation wished to see him, he I had no idea that it was intended to present him with such handsome plate ; and he heartily thanked the sub- ' scribers,not only for the present itself, but f,r the kind feeling which had prompted it. Whenever he looked up- on it, it weuld bring to his memory, if such a reminder were needed, the good relations which had existed be- tween himself and the Servants of the Company, and those conney.ted with the Company. He was only sorry he had to leave Runcorn. He had always endea- voured to do his best for the Company and for those unnder him, and they had always worked comfortably together. In conclusion he again thanked them for their gitt,and expressed the hope that the staff would work as loyally ana well Tor lus successor, Mr. J. Rhodes, of Stafford, as they had done for him.—Mr. W. Howard (foreman porter), and Mr. Ebbrell (manager of book- stall), added their testimony to Mr. Smith's personal character and ability, and the proceedings concluded.
A VICTIMISED THEATRICAL COMPANY.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Mon- day morning, Mr. Townsend, acting manager for Mr. T.B. Leslie's" Up to Time" burlesque company which had been performing at the Warrington Theatre Royal during the last week, applied under the cii cumqances hereafter detailed, for some relief for the actresses belonging to that company. Mr. Townsend said that the ladies had been brought down from London by a man who called himself Leslie. They opened at Warrington last Monday, and worked on throughout the week. On Saturday night, after the performance, Leslie disappeared, taking with him the whole of the week's takings, and leaving them without any pay. He (Mr. Townsend) did not apply on behalf of the actors, as they would be able to shift for themselves, but he would like to know if something could not be done for the ladies. The magistrates heartily sympathised with the unfortunate company—Mr.Monks subscribing £1 and Mr. Hayward 2s,sd.—andalso made a donation ca £1 10s. from the pour box, for tile distressed actresses. It also transpired that the missing manager had left some properties at the theatre, but the manage- ment refused to allow them to be taken away. There had been twenty-three in the company, a few of them being brought from Newcastle, and the rest from London. Leslie, who is altogether unknown in the theatrical world, had promised every one of them an engagement of not less than eighteen weeks. The salaries for the six actresses should have been £lO between theta, it being a joint engagement. One of the actors cordially thanked the magistrates for their kind consideration and assist- ance. Mr. Taylor, police court missionary, and the police, subsequently made a collection on behalf of the unfortunate actresses, and they were enabled to proceed to London.
THE LATE MR. R. LEA OF RUNCORN.

FUNERAL SERMON. On Sunday evening, at Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, the Rev. Dr. Preston, vicar, preached a sermon with special reference to the death of Mr. R. Lea, of Little Sutton, near Chester, who resided for half a century in Runcorn. The rev, gentleman based his discourse on 1. Corinthians xv. 56. After dealing with the lessons to be gathered from the text,he , said a more worthy townsman and truer patriot could not be found. Though not a native of Runcorn became there as a boy, and for years occupied a responsible and important post in her Majesty's service. Be was a man of unblemished character. He was upright, straightforward, honest, conscientious. There was no , double-facedness about him. He was not one to say ill, and to slander behind one's back. Had he fault to find, he would speak kindly face to face. As a public man not one ever accused liim,or could accuse him of a wrong action or base deed. He was a devoted husband, fond father, faithful friend. In matters ecclesiastical he was a staunch Churchman, but large-hearted, liberal-minded and without bigotry. Of that church he was a main pillar and generous supporter, willing to do what in him lay for its maintenance, its welfare, and its progress. He was connected with it from its first opening. He held high office in it. He was vicar's warden for 20 or 30 years. Before the church was built he was an attached and earnest Sunday school teacher ; and for very many years he was manager and treasurer of the day schools. He was one who felt lie had a duty to perform towards man, and a work to do for God. He fully realised his responsibility, and that it was his duty to do what he could for his Master and for the special benefit of others. He had lost a valued friend. Their church had lost a hearty benefactor. Runcorn had lost a noble and esteemed townsman.

div.head: HALTON CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: HALTON CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The annual meeting for the distribution of prizes to the children took place on Sunday afternoon, when the report of the school was read by the Sec- retary (Mr. B. Haddock). This showed there were 115 in the boys' school and 81 in the girls, with a staff of 47 male teachers and 27 female, with an average of attendance for the scholars of 138 and of teachers 44, which was considered very satisfactory. The sick club in connection with the school was in a flourishing condition, there having been placed in the bank to the credit of the club more money than in any one year during the last ten years. The Clothing Club was also doing well. The library in connection with the school is well and ably worked. During the last twelve months there had been a men's Bible class started, and it had grown so rapidly that it now numbered 47 mem- bers on the books. A Sunday afternoon class for young women and girls was very well managed by Mrs. Wray, and was largely attended. On the whole, the school was never known to be so well managed and in a more flourishing condition than it now is. After the reading of the report, the prizes, to the number of about 60, were distributed by Lady Brooke,who said she was very pleased to be with them, for she had once been a Sunday school teacher herself, and when she was able had taken a warm interest in it. She hoped the parents of the children would see that their children were sent re- gularly and punctually to school, as by so doing they would be helping the managers very much. The Vicar said that he was pleased to tell them that the manage- ment ot the school having been taken up by so many volunteers had coriSid-erably helped him in his work,and that the school was never in a better position than it was now. A vote of thanks was proposed by the Super- intendent, Mr. J. W. Haddock, and seconded by Mr.J. Hancock, to Lady Brooke for so kindly coining to give the prizes, and was replied to by Sir R. M. Brooke, Bart. He said he was very pleased to be there,and to see such a marked improvement in the school, and especially in the Men's Bible Class. This brought a very happy and enjoyable afternoon, both to children and parents, to a close.

div.p: Rettrrs to tin cantor.

BUDDHISM AND CHRISTIANITY. Sir,—Owing to pressure of work I have not bad time to reply to Mr. Dignum's letter of Saturday last. I will do so next week. Let me assure him, however, that lam quite as honest in what I write as he is—and I think more so. My letter was not in any way an at- tack on Christianity.—Yours truly, HARRY ESMOND.

THE CHURCH IN WALES. Sir,—The clergy at the Convocations of York and Westminster are up in arms, dreading the coming storm of disestablishing the Church and disendowing the same. But have not the electors good cause for taking these unfaithful stewards to account, men who pledged them- selves" to be ready with all faithful diligence to banish and drive away false doctrine and erroneous teaching contrary to Gud's Word." Alas ! it is clearly trans- parent their hypocrisy is assumed in many cases, solely to secure the loaves and fishes,witness the Roman Catho- lic processions (illegal) of the Guild of Our Lady of Ran- som to Llandaff Cathedral last week, touching the effigy of St. Telw with their rosary beads. We hear not a word of protest from the bishop, he, however, can shout about the Suspensory Bill even without having read it. The same remark applies to the Dean of Westminster. In Cheshire we hear Bishop Jayne in his clerical charge, advocating outdoor sports on Sunday. The laity are perfectly justified in withdrawing their support from such men. They need not be told, "if you do not like the sacerdotal ceremonies, go elsewhere," this, the laity are doing in numbers, and when an appeal for disestab- lishment is made, the electers will rise and sweep this rottenness away. One can clearly see written over the portals of the door of the once Protestant Reformed Church of England February 14, 1893.
ICHABOD.

THE APPOINTMENT OF THE UNION BAKER. Sir,—lt is on the behalf of the Warrington Branch of the Amalgamated Union of Operative Bakers and Con- fectioners that I wish to draw your attention to the above subject. I see that out of the many applications that were made to fill the vacancy caused by the dis- missal of Mr. Cliffe, the baker at the Workhouse, four were appointed to attend the meeting of the Board of Guardians last Wednesday, and they appointed a man named Powell of Hereford. Who in the first place had sent for the successful applicant? Someone who is con- nected with the Board must have done so ; he would never have come the distance he has without being sent for, that is very evident. I feel very sorry, Mr. Editor, that we have members on the Board who could so easily cast aside one of our ewn fellow townsmen, one I know who has been a rate- payer all his life in this town. There is no doubt but that there has been some undue influence used on the part of some one or other, and when the men have en- tered the room for selection, the minds of the Guardians had already been made up. I don't know how they could so easily look over the Warrington men, if such is not the case, for I am sure the man we sent had as good a reference as anyone need wish for, in fact from the leading men of the town. Surely because the man had been out of employment some little length of time was no detriment ? But because Powell was recommended by" One of our officers," he must be elected. I don't presume to dictate Mr. Editor, but I think that if the majority of the Board of Guardians would only use a little of their own discretion and study their own follow- townsmen more, instead of allowing their minds to be biased by officials there would be a deal more satisfac- tion among the ratepayers. Betore I conclude I may say as a Society we have sup- plied a baker time after time when Cliffs has been off work,and now the time has come that a constant man is needed they not only appoint a noi-union'man but one who is a complete stranger to the town. Is he so much superior that there isn't one in the town of Warrington who could fill the vacancy without introducing a "foreigner ?" Surely the ratepayers cannot but feel in- dignant at the action of the Board of Guardians over this affair, and I hope and trust that when the time comes round again that the members seek re-election the ratepayers will do their utmost to throw such men out, for men who will not support their own townsmen are surely not fit to hold the post they do. Thanking you in anticipation for the insertion of the abeve, I beg to remain, Sir,—Yours faithfully, W. BATHBONE. Secretary Stockton Heath, Warrington.
Secretary of Bakers Society.

div.head: MAGAZINES, &c.
div.p: MAGAZINES, &c.

We have received the first number of "The West- minster Budget," a publication which aims at com- bining the best qualities of a newspaper with those of a picture book; and in doing so has succeeded admirably. It is published every Thursday (price 6d.), and is conducted by the late Editor and artis- tic staff of "The Pall Mall Budget." The " English Illustrated Magazine" for February contains a striking portrait of Mr. John Morley, and an accom- panying 'character sketch written by that most capable writer, Mr. Henry W. Lucy. It also con- tains the first chapters of a new serial, a short com- plete story, and several illustrated articles both instructive and amusing. "The Strand Magazine" still keeps up its reputation of being one of the most popular productions or the day. There is so much variety in it, everything being calculated to please both old and young; the interest in it being well sustained throughout. From the same office we have to band a new sixpenny monthly entitled "The Picture Magazine" edited by the same editor —Mr. George Newnes. It is charmingly and variedly illustrated, containing" Fine Art Pictures," "Comic Pictures" some of them by .George Cruik- shank, "Portraits" of popular novelists and artists, some most amusing "Pictures for Children," "Auto- graphs," "Pictures of Places," dtc. It is a com- panion to "The Strand," and has reached the second number. "Our Earth and its Story" by Dr. Robert Brown, M.A., F.R.G.S., F.L.S., is the name of one of Cassell's latest issues. Part I, ready January 25th, includes a Large Tinted Presentation Plate, printed separately, entitled "Icebound," and an abundance of wood engravings which make the narrative mare attractive and interesting. The pleasant style in which it is written is sure to make it popular, and the abundance of information it contains combines the researches of many scientific men. •

div.head: NEGLECTING TO NOTIFY SMALLPDX AT WARRINGTON. A WIDOW PROSECUTED.
div.p: NEGLECTING TO NOTIFY SMALLPDX AT WARRINGTON. A WIDOW PROSECUTED.

At the Borough Court yesterday (Alderman Wright in the chair), a widow named Hannah Six- smith of 25, Glasshouse Row, was charged with neglecting to notify a case of smallpox, which had occurred in her house. Mr. L. Whittle, Town Clerk, appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Corporation. The defendant did not appear in court. Mr. Whittle stated that on Saturday, the 4th of Febru- ary, Dr. Gornall, Medical Officer of Health, visited the defendant's house, in consequence of information he had received. Be there found one of defendant's daughters, aged 19, suffering from smallpox. Several 'cases had occurred in the same street, and there was no doubt that both the defendant and her daughter knew what the latter was suffering from. The defendant, however, was guilty of further negligence. The rash appeared on the previous Tuesday, and after that the defendant allowed two of her children to go to a tea party, this creating a danger of the spread of the in- fection. As the defendant did not appear, he asked for a penalty to be inflicted ;h did not wish for a heavy I penalty, however, as the defendant was a poor woman with a large family. Dr. Gornall next gave evidence, swearing with up- lifted hand. He corroborated Mr. Whittles' statement, and also added that when he saw the girl she admitted that her mother had known when the rash appeared , what she was suffering from. Mr. Whittle pointed out that the ignorance of the law had probably had much to do with the offence. The defendant was fined 10s.,the Chairman remarking that the Bench inflicted that small penalty in conse- quence of Mr. Whittle pointing out the defendant's poor condition. •

div.head: TO ENGLAND AND BACK. VISITING THE OLD COUNTRY.
div.p: TO ENGLAND AND BACK. VISITING THE OLD COUNTRY.
The writer of the following account of a journey "To England and Back in the Winter Season " re- sides in Toronto, Canada, but is the son of a gentle- man well known in Warrington.

To travel alone is not pleasant, so I naturally en- deavoured to find a companion, which at such a time of the year and for such a distance did not prove the easiest of tasks. But after laying my views before a btother Englishman he finally consented to accompany me, and later we were agreeably surprised to find a third party willing to joia us, going on the principle " the more the merrier," our pair was speedily increased to:9. trio. The date of departure was arranged, the selec- tion of steamship made, then commenced final prepara- tion for that much talked of voyage.

As the train glided slowly out of the station it would ' be hard to say what our respective thoughts wers dur- ing the short silence that ensued—there is something of a feeling of solemnity after a farewell. We were soon roused from our reverie and as we locked at each other decided unanimously that our object was to be" Phan —new word dug up out of the seat of a grand trunk car. Toronto may be a fairly large city-, but to get to a much larger one in New York State, where we proposed to embark, we had to pass through Hamilton. The cry all:change here for Niagara Falls Buffalo, and New York, rang through the cars. We Obeyed and were soon ensconsed in the private section of a luxurious parlour car. " Pliun " commenced and ere we realized it we were on United States border. Just as a matter of business, though of course sorry to give the trouble, Uncle Sam's custom's men would like to see the style of our clothing and any bric-a-brac we might have care- fully packed away in our saratogas, for the amusement of the baby in England. But like many other men, his bark is far worse than his bite, and with the greatest courtesy, and little trouble to ourselves, we notice the mystic chalk characters placed upon our packages, and ' we are free to wander to any part of the States.

There being no dining car attached to the train, the coloured gentleman wished to know if we would like dinner at Buffalo, being now pretty late nothing would please us better. Man may live without love, what is passion but pining ? But where is the man that can live without dining' Upon arrival there we hurried to the dining hall, the proprietor looked somewhat astonishcd, and whilst we and others were explaining what our craving was—in walks the boy with the telegram. There had been a big delay somewhere and we poor passengers were the sufferers. So making a hasty meal cf such viands as were obtainable, we hurried back to our car and soon after retired for the night.

We were due in Jersey City at 8 a.m., but ere that time we were enjoying the sight of a beautiful sunrise on the mountains. The scenery all around was very pic- turesque, the track of the Erie R.R. being laid by the side of a river flowing at the foot of a high mountain range. Very similar to the Hudson river and the Catskill mountains. That reminds me of the story of a South- erner on hoard a New York Central car upon first seeing an ice-boat racing alongside the train. Southerner : How thick is that ice out there? Troy Citizen : About two feet, I think, Southerner : By jove, you must have some holy old breezes up here to send a boat through it like that there one's going.

With a fair wind the ice-boats on the Hudson can keep up to an express train. They are borne upon the surface of the ice upon iron runners, so that very little resistance or friction is offered to impede their progress, obtained by the use of sails like an ordinary boat. They are used as a means of transit, but mostly for pleasure, and the experiences gone through in the first journey make lasting impressions.

But we are passing house after house and fast leaving the river and mountains behind us, and just prior to eight o'clock arrive at Jersey City. Here we take the ferry steamer across north-river to New York City— what a busy scene presents itself! The river appears alive with numerous steamers, ferry boats, small tug boats towing immense barges loaded with several rail- way cars or perhaps cargo in transit from steamer to quay or vica versa. On every side the screech of the whistle is heard and as steamer rushes by steamer it is wonderful there a-e not more accidents than reported. Steamers and large sailing vessels ride majestically at anchor in mid stream. Leaving the boat at Chambers- st. and having seen to our baggage, as we emerge. num- erous cab drivers persecute us with requests to drive us round the city, to our hotel, Szc., kc., but in New York like most other places, we found it wiser to make a bar- gain ere we placed a foot upon the Jehu's sacred property finally making our selection, with a bow our driver , decided to accept just one half of what he first asked. To the " Metropoltan " is our order. After rattling down many dark, dirty, noisy streets, vv.., emerge on Broadway and are soon within the hall of ti:e hotel— then to breakfast leisurely partaken of, a few letters to friends left behind, and we are on our way to view the steamer that is to carry us acrcss the Atlantic.

Mounting on the vessel's deck we are at once impressed with the grandeur and immense proportions of this mighty leviathan of the deep—the "Teutonic" of the White Star Line. Perhaps after sailing, rather than now, an account would help to relieve the every day routine of an ocean voyage. So leaving a few small packages, kc., in charge of the Company's servants we I left the noisy quay and proceeded to the city.

To one who has never been in a large busy city New York must almost make them remain still and lose them- !elves in silent wonderment. For suppose one is stand- ing on Broadway, viewing the enormous vehicular traffic passing up and down. How forcibly the story is brought before 000 of the English country gentleman upon his first visit to London. He being desirous of crossing Lothbury had stood in the front of the Bank of England so long that a policeman asked him, what he wanted, he quietly replied to cross the street but was waiting for the pr,cession to end—l wonder if that county gentleman is waiting yet I Our stay in this the greatest port of America was but of short duration for our steamer sailed at seven a.m. next morning, and as one of our party had never been here before sight-seeing was foremost on our programme. And extended trips on the elevated railway gave a very fair idea of certain portions of the city; a street car ride up Broadway the opportunity of seeing the many fine stores and business houses; a short walk to Brooklyn Bridge showed the dirty, narrow, ill-paved streets and upon nearing East River of the squalor and poverty that existed there.

Towering high above us is that lasting monument of 19th century engineering skill, Brooklyn Bridge. Feeling that some knowledge regarding the same would be benefi- cial, upon making inquiries we learn that the enorm- ous towers on either side of the roof are built of solid masonry and 276 feet above the surface of the water, each are pierced by two arches of great size, being 120 feet high. The sinking of the foundations caused many deaths chiefly from caison disease arising from bad gas, but most lamentably that of the engineer, Mr. John A. Roebling, who died from lockjaw resulting from a crushed foot received when superintending the laying of one of the piers. 'the work was proceeded with under the supervision of his son, who was also destined like many of the workers to be a victim of caison disease from which he did not recover, but through his wife gave the instructions necessary for the completion of the work. The total length of the bridge is 5,989 feet, the New York approach being 1,562 i feet, Brooklyn 972 A., and the suspended structure 3,454 feet. The centre span is 135 feet above high water mark and mea- sures 1,595 feet. The four cables are 16 inches in dia- meter, each containing about 5,090 single wires, the total weight of material is between 6 and 7,000 tons. There are five avenues, two central ones fetr cars, which are drawn by an endless steel wire cable, the two outer ones being reserved for vehicles, whilst suspended over- head is a broad promenade for pedestrians. The traffic across the bridge is enormous as statistics taken Thurs- day, January 10th, 1888, go to show, that from 12 o'clock midnight 32,900 crossed from New York to Brooklyn, and from the latter to New York 37.363, making a total of 61,130 persons in 24 hours. From the centre of this magnificent structure a fine view is obtained of the ship- ping on either side of east river and thei city of Brook- lyn this latter resembles New York n many respects, the streets being wider, handsome stores and many residences, being' the homes of New York's busy workers.

Taking the car back asross the bridge the produce exchange is visited where through the kindness of one of the members we are piloted round the room, a large and lofty one, on various tables are shown samples of cereals flour and other products. Telegraph reports are con- tinually coming in and a large business is done in "spot "and " futures." At times great excitement is manifested as cram n may advance a few points or per- haps decline. Leaving the exchange where" merchants most do congregate" entering the elevator, passing floor after floor, we are soon landed on top of the exchange but not of the tower, another elevator runs to the top of the tower. As we yass out what a grand panoramer is presented before us. At.a height equal to 16 storeys nothing obstructed our view, beneath us lay the great city, a dull murmer of general confused noises as of voices, traffic, Szc. On either side the two rivers bounded by Brooklyn and Jersey city—in front Governor's Island, a little to the right Bartholdi's statue of Liberty, whilst beyond in the far distance the broad Atlantic lay. Much as we would, we could not linger, for what is a day to view such a large city. Descend- ing to the ground floor and thanking our friend for his kindness and courtesy, we made our exit to the street. More car rides, more sights, a few purchases and then a short season of rest followed by a tramp around town in the evening.
All passengers were supposed to be on board the " Teutonic " that night, which gave anyone

div.head: EXAMINER., SAT URD AY, FEI3II UAIIY 18, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER., SAT URD AY, FEI3II UAIIY 18, 1893.

unaccustomed to steamer berths an opportunity to feel at home, prior to being tossed about on the mighty deep. We were all tired and very soon after retiring were sound asleep. An alarm clock was quite unnecessary next morning for with the washing of decks and general work of putting everything in its place there was quite enough noise to awaken the soundest sleeper. There being considerable excitement attending the departure of a steamer, we hurried through our toilet and were sood on deck. Oh, but such a morning, a heavy leg hung ever the water, and to still make matters worse small drizzling rain was descending—a veritable Scotch mist.

Prior to sailing a cause of some little anxiety comes to everyone, that is as to whether ones baggage is all on board, then the list of packages is gone over, and a full knowledge that the large saratoga was put in the bag- gage room of the steamer marked "Wanted on voy- age," another is consigned to the hold the " not wanted "label being affixed : then the Gladstone bag labelled "State Room "a small hand bag, a bundle of sticks, umbrellas. kc., a steamer's rug, a brown paper parcel, then the light paper package of suspicious form; a bundle of newspapers, novels, Etc., perhaps a bunch of flowers—all may be carried by several friends. Then ones own burden may consist of a spare overcoat or wrapper and a few more packages of pre- sents for friends on the other side. All these have to go to the Stateroom, until that cabin with all its pack- ages strewn about looks more like a railway dep6t bag- gage room than a hibitual abode of 2 or 3 maybe 4 persons for nearly a week. As you are looking round in silent wonderment, and planning where this or that can be put, your companion for the voyage comes alung with an equal amount of goods and chattels, until you feel almost like giving up in despair of sleeping any- where but on the floor, for your berth is by this time quite filled with your numerous packages. A knock is heard at the door and as the next party steps in still a few more of the necessities for comfort Asc., on an ocean trip are brought along and placed upon the 3rd parties berth. If nearly giving up in despair before, it is al- most a case of total collapse now, and you are wishing you had never proposed the trip, or at any rate left a few " trinkets" behind. As another knock is heard you are almost speechless for a gentleman enquires is this 42. "Kes "from within, " Then I guess this is my room berth, N 0.4." Where can he ever find room for bag- gage ? So far as he is concerned you are at rest almost immediately,sl for upon looking round quietly for a minute he says— "l guess you gentlemen are going for a long stay abtoad." "Why so ?" " Well, what about these boxes, valises, bags, parcels, bundles, packages, etc." "Haven't you some baggage coming in ?''

" Well I guess not." "What do you take when travelling ?" "Generally a hat box and umbrella. The former carries my hat,:linen, etc., the latter keeps of the sun or rain." The foregoing is just an imaginary, yet daily scene on board the ocean steamers. Upon making inquiries, we assured, indeed saw all our various packages in their respective places. So our cause for anxiety was at an end concerning our baggage. (To be continued.)
eport. The minutes were approved on the motion of Ah3erman Timmins, seconded by Councillor Single- ton,

FINANCE.—THE BOROUGH RATE. The Finance Committee reported that the Borough ac- countant had produced the estimate of the amount re- quired by the Council for the year ending the 25th March, 1894, in aid of the borough fund for the pur- pose of defraying the expenses of executing .he several Acts of Parliament for the regulation of and relating to municipal corporations. The estimate included incor- poration expenses, £405 83. Bd. ; preparation, tsc. of burgess lists £lB6 4s. ; first municipal election, £245 17s. 9d. ; second municipal election, £72 15s. 7d. ; armorial bearings, £l2O ; election of councillors and borough auditors and preparation of burgess lists, 1893, £2BO ; School Board, one year's precept, £5,000 ; free library, one years estimate, £550 ; technical instruction, one year's estimate, £150; town clerk's depart- ment, £487 16s. ; police for the borough £1,535 ; town hall department, £1,344 Os. ; salaries, £369; Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, £5B. ; Sale of Food and Drugs Act; £l2 ; total, £10,796 2s. 9d., receipts, £243 16s. leaving the net amount required .210,552. It was resolved that the estimate be approved and adopted by the Council, and that a precept for the amount stated be served upon the overseers. Re- solved that the salaries of Mr. Woodend and F, Teasdale be advanced as follows. viz., Mr. Woodend to £125 per annum, F. Teesdale to 103 per week ; and that the ar- rangement made by the late Local Board with reference to the salary of Mr. D. Martin be adhered to. Councillor Owens, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said there were a number of items included in the borough rate which were formerly included in the poor rate. There was a School Board precept of £5,000 and there Was £1,535 for the police of the borough, £58.1 for the Contagious Diseases Act (Animals), and 2,12 for Food and Dregs Act, making £6,605 which was formerly included in the poor rate. The other items were formerly included in the district rate. It would be observed that the cost of incorporation and elections amounted to 21,030.—Councillor Bullough seconded the motion.— Councillor Shuttleworth asked on what proportion of that rate agricultural land would have to pay. He also observed that there were three items of £5O put down for the Acting 'Town Clerk.—Councillor Owens said the General Purposes Committee had voted the Acting Town Clerk £l5O for his services in connection with the incor- poration matters,and it had been divided into three parts. Agricultural land would have to pay its full assessment in the borough rate. A thousand pounds of the estimate was expenditure that would not occur again.—The minutes were carried. THE GIFTS TO THE TOWN.

Councillor F. Neil said before moving the minutes of the Technical Instruction Committee, 'he should like to refer to what was in the minds of the people of the town and no dbubt of the members of the Council. While

not strictly within the province -of the Council, he thought it was to some extent the place of the Technical Instruction Committee as an educational committee to take some notice ot the generous gifts of Mr. Timmis and the Mayor. eHear, hear) The very generous gift of £2,500 by Mr. Timmis would stimulate education in the elementary schools, and they could not help but acknowledge the breadth of his offer for it was not con- fined to any particular school, but it was open to all. ' Farther, the Mayor's gift would stimulate those who had perhaps taken the scholarships so kindly provided by Mr. Timmis, to still pursue their studies in the Univer- sity College, Liverpool. Ile moved that the Town Council thank T. S. Timmis Esq., and his Worship the Mayor for their very generous gifts in the cause of edu- cation in Widnes. Mr. T. Smith seconded the motion, which was put by the Town Clerk and carried by acclamati4m.—The Mayor on behalf of Mr. Timmis and Isimself thanked the Council for their recogn;tion of what they had done. They believed that what they had done was for the benefit of Widnes in the widest sense, that was by helping to forward the education of the place.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AD
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AD
A ETILETICS.
FOOTBALL.

There are many things which are difficult to account for. Amongst them I am going to include the way Warrington lost the match with 'fyidesley on Saturday. That is something which requires accounting for. I with many others can cast a faint light upon it ; I with others can modestly point out what is believed to be the octopus which is sucking out the sap and strength of the club. Yes, sap; it is a useful expression. It is a pliable verbal rod, wherewith to point out my meaning ; it is the essence of my theory for I believe that it is " sap- py" play which is to account for the whole mirerable business.

But, before proceeding with a criticism of the actual match, let me pause for a momentary categorising of the items of bad play which go to make" sappy " play. First there is individual selfishness ; there is indifferent, nay, bad org anisation ; and there is overdone self-con- fidence which has been the parent of indolence and care- lessness. All these are charges which I repeat as being laid at the door of the W. F. C. by many of their admirers. And never did I see those evils exempli- fied more copiously than on Saturday; and never did I see a Warrington " Gate" more disappointed with their home team—or see simple ardent admirers, whose rude speech was filled with allegories and metaphors,so rude in their quaintness, and so rude in their pronunciation. It made me blush, for almost every metaphor applied to Warrington play had a big, big, D in it.

Now the most suprising part of the thing is, that in the first half of the game, when the visitors had almost a gale of wind blowing behind them, the Warrington team played faultessly and against tremendous odds did a successful defensive game. They prevented the visitors from scoring. What was the result. The spirits of Warrington people got rather high, of course they didn't know wky, and above the winds bleak sigh, you could see your most staide and elderly friends shouting " Oh, my, hi-tid-li-hi " which they accompanied by throwing their hats at the air, an I bursting their elastic stockings by: trying to dance. These joyous spirits, flying so quickly into the hyperean realms of ectsacy, had, so to speak to" dumb ' down again.

Very well And how was it done you say? It was done very smartly, so far as Tyldesley went. When the second half commenced odds were pretty heavy on Warrington. But the angel of Warrington's triumph was evidently out to tea, because she didn't turn up ; she never does now, somehow, she ought to get notice to quit. F.ach fleeting minute after the restart brought with it a deeper colour to the contrast that was form. lug between the play of the homesters,in the two halves. The first half had been one piece of brilliant defence ; the second half, when the odds were for us, was one piece of hard individual play, but without general or- ganisation, without unison, without anything indeed but "mull "and indescriminate play. In the packs the fowards were just up a stump, and the four three- quarters (vide Welsh system) were either nowhere or up a gum stick. Why did they attempt to play the Welsh style in a competition without having had previous practice ?

P. R. Lawless played a very fast game, and a very good one too. Presently he will become celebrated as a "tackler," if he leaps over 80 many fellows' heads, and brings so many players low. His brother, T. Lawless, made a promising debut at centre. He did some smart kicking. J. Jolley was up to the front in good style, whilst his brother-county man Boscow, played a sur- prisingly good game, which showed how fit he is for county honours. Webster,as the likeliest scorer on several occasions, was much neglected.

Our local team played off a fixture with Dewsbury on Shrove Tuesday, at Dewsbury. From what I can hear they Played a game 20 per cent, better than the compe- tition match on Saturday, and they secured three tries to a drop goal and a try.

I was glad to see that Boscow gave ample satisfaction in the discharge of his onerous duties bathe county match on Wednesday. The most reliable critics described his play as "excellent—all round." The game is reported to have been a very fast one. It resulted in a win for Lancashire by a goal and a try, to three tries.

St. Helens Recs. met Swinton on Saturday, in the competition, and they fared better than Warrington did with the leaders of the score list. The match ended in a draw. I knew it would be a draw when I saw the two teams had to meet. It drew one of the largest gates of the season. The results of the competition up to date are :
